        <h3>Reporter's Notebook (TF)</h3>
        <div class="meta">A diary · Featherquill working notes, half-redacted · Year 35 mid-season</div>
        <p><em>Day 1.</em> Editor wants 600 words on the field-widening for Quarterly. Asked me to be opinionated. I am, by training, opinionated. The deadline is fine. The reporting is the harder part. The Rules Committee will not return calls. They never return calls. I will draft from secondary sources and re-interview when they break. The bulletin language is unusually plain. They are embarrassed. People are reliable when they are embarrassed.</p>
        <p><em>Day 2.</em> Talked to two coaches. Wolves' staff are upset. Otters' staff are euphoric. Talked to one Sniper anonymously — said she had not realized how often she had been firing from spawn until she watched her own film, and that the realization was uncomfortable. She said the wider field "feels like the sport waking up after a long nap." I will not use this quote on the record. It is too good and she will be punished for it. I will paraphrase.</p>
        <p><em>Day 4.</em> The Cultural Office's Reno paper leaked. Junior columnist at this paper got it. I did not get it. I am not bitter. I am, however, going to do my own draft of the Reno piece for next quarter, because the leaked version is more polish than reporting and the actual files have more in them. The intern who leaked it is a friend of an old friend. I will not name them in print but I will buy them a sandwich.</p>
        <p><em>Day 5.</em> Filed the field-widening column. Editor cut my line about "tactical phase that had been eroding." Said it was preachy. Editor was right. Replaced with: "the rounds are now slower at the start, and that is a thing the rounds were missing, and which the new rounds have." Editor said this was worse. I disagreed. I disagreed in writing. We compromised on neither version and wrote a third. The third is fine. I do not love the third. I love the second.</p>
        <p><em>Day 7.</em> Watched a full match on the new field. The opening sixty seconds of round one were a slow advance — both Snipers walking forward, neither in range, both visibly uncomfortable about not being in range. The Brawlers got there first. The Brawlers were excited about getting there first. The crowd noticed. The crowd was excited that the Brawlers were excited. I do not have an editorial position on this. I am writing it down because it felt good to watch.</p>
        <p><em>Day 9.</em> A knight emailed me. They had read the Quarterly column. They wrote: "thank you for not assuming we were already happy." I did not assume that. I do not, in general, assume that. The knight asked to remain anonymous. I have honored the request. I am writing this in a private notebook so the request stays honored.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Talia Featherquill, working notes, archived under journalist privilege</div>
      </article>

      <article class="diary">
        <h3>Working Journal — A Coyote Speedster (CYT)</h3>
        <div class="meta">A diary · Sonora high-desert basin · Year 36 founding-bell pre-season</div>
        <p><em>Tuesday.</em> Coach Reyes asked me to keep a working journal this season. The other Speedsters do not keep journals. The other Speedsters do not, by my read, write much at all. Reyes thinks the team needs at least one written internal record so that when we win something the league archivists can be told, with documentation, how we won it. I am writing the journal. I am the most-literate of the active line, by Reyes's measure, which I appreciate as a compliment but which I also suspect is the thinnest possible compliment our roster could field.</p>
        <p><em>Wednesday.</em> Drilled the drift today. The drift is the simplest tactic we run and also the most-respected. The drift is: <em>I appear to retreat.</em> I appear to retreat unhurriedly. I do not run; running marks me. I lope. I lope away from a center engagement. The opposing team, watching, registers that one Coyote is leaving the engagement. The opposing team's attention narrows toward the four Coyotes still in the engagement. I take a wide arc — wider than I would need to take if I were actually retreating — around the perimeter, behind a piece of cover that the opposing team's attention is not currently on, and I hold there. I am, at this point, no longer a knight in the opposing team's tactical map. I am erased. Reyes calls this <em>la borradura</em>. I am erased.</p>
        <p>The other four Coyotes, while I am being erased, are running their own drifts in their own arcs. By two minutes into the round, on a clean execution, the opposing team's tactical map shows an empty pitch with one Coyote engaged at the center and they are, at this point, badly mistaken about where their threats are. By two minutes and ten seconds, on a clean execution, six of us hit them from six positions, including the one Coyote at the center, who has, by this point, drifted out and back in. We do not, technically, have a sixth knight. The sixth Coyote is the field's perception of how many of us there are. Reyes calls this <em>el sexto</em>. The sixth.</p>
        <p><em>Thursday.</em> I asked Reyes whether the drift would still work in Year 36 now that the Caucus's Commitment Directive has formalized into a coaching standard across all teams. Rule One of the Directive is <em>"Commit to a heading for at least eight strides before reconsidering."</em> The drift requires opposing knights to redirect attention frequently — it depends on their attention being movable. If they're committing to a heading for eight strides at a time, the drift may have less to bait against.</p>
        <p>Reyes laughed. Reyes does not laugh often. Reyes said: <em>"The Directive will make every team better at walking. Every team but us. We have always walked correctly. The Directive describes our default. The Directive does not, however, address attention."</em> Then Reyes said: <em>"The drift is not about how the opposing team walks. The drift is about how the opposing team thinks about the pitch. The Directive does not change how teams think about the pitch. The Directive only changes how they walk on it. We are still going to be erased. We are still going to be six."</em> I wrote this down because it was, frankly, the clearest tactical instruction I have received in two seasons.</p>
        <p><em>Friday.</em> Met with the Antlerlords' coaching staff for a pre-season tactical exchange. We had been told this would be a one-hour meeting. It was four hours. The Antlerlords have one tactic. The tactic is: <em>"L'Ancrage stands. We rotate."</em> Their entire pre-season tactical packet is forty pages long, and thirty-six of those pages are about <em>which direction to rotate around the Anchor depending on which kind of opposing team we are facing.</em> When the Antlerlords were asked, in this meeting, what they would do against the drift, their head coach paused for forty-five seconds and then said: <em>"We would, I think, rotate slightly faster. The Anchor would not move. We have not yet faced this. We will think about it more."</em> I appreciate the honesty. I do not, however, look forward to playing them. I am told L'Ancrage is the size of a small building. Coach Reyes thinks the drift will still work, on the grounds that <em>"a building is a piece of cover; we run drifts around cover; this is, in fact, easier."</em> I want to believe this.</p>
        <p><em>Saturday.</em> Founding bell tomorrow. We open the season against the Pittsburgh Ravens. The Ravens' Snipers are, by Caucus record, the most-decorated archery class in the League. The drift is hardest to run against Snipers because Snipers do not need to redirect attention to track us — they have already tracked us. Reyes said tonight, at the team meal, that the drift will be modified for round one: we will scatter rather than drift, on the grounds that scattering creates more sniper-targeting decisions per second than drifting does, and the Ravens' Snipers will, with five targets to range, choose the wrong target at least once per round. The drift will return, in modified form, by round three when the Ravens' Snipers have settled.</p>
        <p>I asked Reyes how he knew the Ravens' Snipers would settle by round three. Reyes said: <em>"They settle by round three because that is when their bench tells them to settle. Their bench tells them to settle in round three because the bench has noticed, by then, what we are doing. We are giving the bench three rounds of misinformation. The fourth round is the round we win. We will lose the first three. We will lose them by tight margins. We will, in the fourth, win by a clean four-on-three. Trust me on this."</em> I do not, in fact, fully trust him on this. I am writing it down so that, after tomorrow, I can come back and check whether he was right.</p>
        <p><em>Sunday — addendum, post-match.</em> Final score Coyotes 3 Ravens 2. We lost rounds one, two, and three by margins of one knight each. We won rounds four and five by clean four-on-three. The fourth round took two minutes and forty seconds. The fifth round took ninety seconds. Reyes did not, after the match, say anything about having predicted this. Reyes simply nodded once at me and went to talk to the Ravens' coach. I did not write down what they said to each other. I do not need to. The journal is for the wins. This is a win.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— working journal, name withheld at coach's request, archived under team privilege at Sonora basin training facility</div>
      </article>

      <article class="diary">
        <h3>A Tank's Camp Notes (BDG)</h3>
        <div class="meta">A diary · Cleveland Boulder Badgers · seven-season Tank veteran · Year 36 training camp, weeks one through four</div>
        <p><em>Week 1, Monday.</em> Camp began with a coach reading the Commitment Directive aloud to the line. All five of us were in the room. All five of us already knew the Directive — every team has had the document since pre-season — but the coach, Brockholm Slatebrush, said he wanted us to hear it together once before camp started. The directive's three rules took him, by my watch, eleven minutes to read aloud, because he stopped after each rule and asked us, individually, what we thought of it. None of us had a strong opinion to offer. Slatebrush is a Tank. We are all Tanks. Tanks do not, as a class, have strong opinions about coaching memos. We have strong opinions about plate. The directive does not address plate.</p>
        <p><em>Week 1, Wednesday.</em> First scrimmage. The line drilled the Commitment Directive's Rule Two — <em>"When you have no target, hold a position. The position is your guard. Do not drift. Pick the position once, hold it for sixty strides, and only then reconsider where to stand."</em> This is, to a Badger, the easiest rule in the document. Our standard tactic is to hold the position until somebody asks us to move it. We held our positions. The scrimmage's opposing line (Speedsters from the practice squad) drifted around us for forty-five minutes and could not, by any approach angle, find an opening. The scrimmage ended in a stalemate. Slatebrush wrote on the practice board, in the team's Year-36 idiom, <em>"holding the floor is the floor"</em> and walked out of the gym without saying anything else. We took this as a compliment.</p>
        <p><em>Week 2, Friday.</em> Wave Doctrine drills today. The Doctrine — the new respawn rule for continuous-mode tournaments — does not, by League rule, apply to deathmatch. Our regular-season schedule is mostly deathmatch. We will, by season schedule, encounter the Doctrine in three matches across the season. Slatebrush had us drill the Doctrine anyway. He said: <em>"The Doctrine is the future. The Caucus will, within four seasons, extend it to deathmatch. We will be drilled. We will be ready. We will not be the team that has to learn the Doctrine in a Final."</em> I think he is right about the Caucus. The Doctrine has, by the Year 36 founding-bell schedule, already produced two come-from-behind wins in continuous-mode matches. The Caucus likes things that produce come-from-behind wins. The Caucus likes the Doctrine. The Caucus will, eventually, extend it.</p>
        <p>The drill was: the line was sent to the bench. The line waited eight seconds. The line returned to the field as a wave, in a four-knight diamond, with the slowest knight (me — Tanks are the slowest in any wave) on a sprint allowance. We crossed the spawn line within two seconds of each other. We hit the center engagement zone within four seconds of each other. The opposing line (the practice squad's Strikers) had, by the moment we arrived, formed a defensive arc that we, in formation, broke through on the first pass. The drill's coach (a Badger named Coach Grimshale, who has not, in nine seasons, ever shown an emotion publicly) said, watching the drill from the gym's elevated platform: <em>"This is, by a margin, the most coordinated thing a Badger line has done in a training camp. I am, frankly, surprised. The Doctrine is going to be good for us."</em> I wrote this in the journal because it is the closest Coach Grimshale has ever come, in my hearing, to being publicly enthusiastic about anything. Slatebrush told me, after the drill, that I should not, in any subsequent journal entry, make Grimshale sound enthusiastic. I am not making him sound enthusiastic. I am, however, recording that he was enthusiastic. The journal is the journal.</p>
        <p><em>Week 3, Tuesday.</em> The team had a closed-door tactical session today on the Antlerlords' L'Ancrage. The Antlerlords are, by season schedule, on our R7 schedule — the third week of the regular season. The Antlerlords' tactic is, in summary, <em>"L'Ancrage stands. We rotate."</em> Our coaching staff has been preparing for this match for, by Slatebrush's frank admission, the entire pre-season. We are a Tank-heavy team. They are a team built around a single Tank who does not move. The natural tactic, for us, against them, is to put our line on their L'Ancrage and dare them to rotate around our line. This is, by Slatebrush's read, what the Antlerlords expect us to do. He has, in the closed-door session, proposed that we do, instead, the opposite — we drift past L'Ancrage as if he is a piece of cover, and we engage their rotating four-knight at the perimeter where they are, by the rotation's geometry, more spread out than they expect to be. He called this <em>"the wide draw."</em> The line was skeptical. The line was also, at the close of the session, willing to drill it. We drilled it for three hours that afternoon. It is not a Badger tactic. It is, by reading, a Coyote tactic. Slatebrush admitted this, said: <em>"The Coyotes call this the drift. We are going to call this the wide draw, because if we call it the drift, we will not be willing to do it. We need to do it. We need to call it something else. The wide draw is what we are going to call it. Do not, in any post-match interview, call it the drift. The Caucus is paying attention. They will publish a paper and we will look like we have been borrowing tactics. We have, in fact, borrowed the tactic. But we will not look it. Do not test this."</em> The line agreed to the framing. The line is going to call it the wide draw. We have not, as a team, ever been told to lie to the Caucus before. We are doing it. It feels strange. It also feels correct.</p>
        <p><em>Week 4, Sunday.</em> Camp ends tomorrow. The Year 36 regular season opens in nine days. I have, as of this entry, drilled the Commitment Directive, the Wave Doctrine, the wide draw, and the standard four-knight Badger floor-hold. The line is more prepared than I have been at any pre-season opening since Year 31. We are, as a team, the oldest line in the League by average season-tenure. We are also, by the analytic services that publish such things, projected to finish fifth in the standings — out of twenty teams, that is the upper quartile but not the championship tier. Slatebrush's response to the projection, at the line meeting yesterday: <em>"Fifth would be the highest finish in Badger team history. The projections do not know we are running the wide draw. The projections do not know how good Coach Grimshale was, last week, at watching the wave drill. The projections are going to be wrong by, I think, two places. We will, by the bracket's end, finish third. Do not tell anyone I said this. The journal does not count."</em> He looked directly at me, when he said the last sentence. He knew about the journal. The whole line knows about the journal. The journal is supposed to be private. The journal is also, apparently, not very private. I will, going forward, write fewer team-strategy quotes from the head coach. I will also, with apologies to Slatebrush, leave this entry intact. The wide draw is the wide draw. He told us, all five of us, in a closed-door session. He knew I would write it down. He also knew the Antlerlords do not read the Badgers' team-internal training-camp journals, because the Antlerlords do not, by their own admission, read anything written in League Common faster than once per word. We have nine days to season-opener. We are, as a line, in a good place. I am going to bed.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— working journal, BDG Tank line · Year 36 training camp · archived under team privilege · "the wide draw" reference subsequently flagged by team comms staff but left intact by author's request</div>
      </article>
    </div>

        <h3>Match Log: Year 36 R2 Crown — RCC vs PLR (Boise Frosthold Pitch)</h3>
        <div class="meta">Official sportscaster transcript · 14:38 game time · Crown-bracket continuous-mode · the Wave Doctrine's second sanctioned application</div>
        <p>00:00 — Crown match opens. Standard Crown rules apply: brass crown spawns at the center pitch; whoever wears it scores team points per second; first team to fifty wins. Wave Doctrine in effect — downed knights return together as a wave on a fixed delay rather than as individuals on rolling timers.</p>
        <p>00:31 — Both teams advance to center. The crown spawns at the eight-second mark; Pell Whittlestone's standard placement. Pickup contest is a four-on-four melee. RCC Brawler Trash Tinker engages the wall from the south. Trash absorbs three plate hits and is downed at 02:18. RCC's first wave-pending knight on the bench.</p>
        <p>02:46 — Score PLR 22 RCC 0. RCC Speedster Drift Brittlepaw, attempting to flank Saltgale from the east, is shot at extreme range by PLR Sniper Frosttooth. Speed-archetype kit absorbs nothing; Brittlepaw down at 02:51. Two RCC knights now wave-pending. The Caucus's Wave Doctrine clock starts.</p>
        <p>03:08 — Score PLR 28 RCC 0. RCC's remaining three knights — captain Trashbright, Healer Featherquill (no relation), and Striker Roundeye — adopt a defensive arc at the south wall. They are not pushing the wall. They are waiting. The crown is, by the LMG broadcast booth's read, a lost cause this minute. The bench is the play.</p>
        <p>03:34 — Score PLR 32 RCC 0. RCC's first wave releases. The wave is the two downed knights — Trash and Brittlepaw — accompanied by Trashbright and Roundeye, who have, on the wave's release, fallen back to spawn to consolidate. (Captain Trashbright's read of the play, per his post-match interview: <em>"the snowball was running. We had to break the snowball. The way to break a snowball is to stop fighting downhill. We fell back. We re-formed. We came up the hill together."</em>) Featherquill, the Healer, remains in the field as RCC's lone defender.</p>
        <p>03:34:08 — The wave forms at RCC's spawn line in a four-knight diamond. Trashbright leads. Trash anchors the rear. Brittlepaw and Roundeye flank. The slowest knight in the wave is Trash, the Tank; the Wave Doctrine grants him a sprint allowance to keep the wave's pace consistent. The wave begins its advance.</p>
        <p>03:48 — Score PLR 38 RCC 0. The wave crosses the eighth-pace line. PLR's wall, having seen the wave form on the broadcast tactical map, is already adjusting. Saltgale (still wearing the crown, still scoring) cannot move; his crown is anchoring his score. The other three Polar Bears begin to spread to engage the wave's flanks.</p>
        <p>04:02 — The wave hits the center engagement zone. Trashbright leads with shield raised. Trash hits the line at full sprint with the Wave Doctrine's allowance still active — he hits PLR Brawler Snowtread square at four-foot range and Snowtread is, by the engagement camera, knocked clean off the crown's outer ring. Snowtread is down at 04:04. PLR's first wave-pending knight.</p>
        <p>04:14 — Brittlepaw and Roundeye engage Frosttooth from two angles. Frosttooth's railgun has tracking time; she is not built for two-target close engagement. She catches Roundeye but Brittlepaw closes the angle and downs her with a paired pistol burst. Frosttooth down at 04:16. PLR's second wave-pending.</p>
        <p>04:23 — Featherquill, the lone RCC Healer, has been steadily moving up the field at a Healer's pace and is, at this point, in mid-court. She does not engage. She stays in cover. She is, per Healer protocol, waiting for a teammate to need her. Trashbright takes a hit from PLR's last standing line knight (Coldcoat, the Tank) and falls back. Featherquill closes to him and heals. Trashbright re-engages.</p>
        <p>04:31 — Saltgale, alone now and still anchoring the crown, recognizes the situation. He has lost three teammates in twenty seconds. He drops the crown. He retreats. The Caucus's Wave Doctrine has, in this engagement, delivered exactly the snowball-break the doctrine was designed for. Score PLR 41 RCC 0 — but the score is no longer ticking. The crown is unattended.</p>
        <p>04:34 — Trash, the RCC Tank, picks up the crown. Trash begins scoring for RCC. Score PLR 41 RCC 1.</p>
        <p>04:48 — PLR's wave forms. Snowtread, Frosttooth, and Saltgale (who has fallen back to spawn to consolidate, the same tactical move RCC made at 03:34) wave-up together in a three-knight wave. Coldcoat and the remaining PLR knight Whitesong are still in the field, contesting Trash. Whitesong is, at this point, in close engagement with Featherquill, who has switched from Healer to defensive harasser — a non-standard role for a Healer but one the Caucus permits when the Healer is the only available defender.</p>
        <p>05:02 — PLR's wave crosses center. The wave is a three-knight chevron with Frosttooth in the rear. The slowest in the wave today is Saltgale, the Brawler, who is on a sprint allowance from the Wave Doctrine. The wave hits the RCC line at full pace. The engagement is short and close.</p>
        <p>05:14 — Featherquill is downed by Whitesong. RCC's first wave-pending knight. Trash drops the crown to engage. Score frozen at PLR 41 RCC 4.</p>
        <p>(transcript continues — abbreviated for archive)</p>
        <p>13:08 — Score PLR 47 RCC 38. Both teams have, over the intervening eight minutes, executed three more wave returns each, with progressively cleaner formations and progressively more decisive engagements. The match has, by the broadcast booth's read, become a back-and-forth contest of wave-vs-wall, neither side able to maintain a sustained crown lead.</p>
        <p>13:42 — RCC's fourth wave forms with all four downed knights plus Trashbright. The wave is, at this point, the largest single return of the match. Wave Doctrine sprint allowance activates on Trash. The wave crosses center as a five-knight phalanx — wider than the diamond, wider than the chevron, the formation Trashbright has personally drawn up on the bench in the prior 80 seconds.</p>
        <p>14:03 — The phalanx engages PLR's depleted line (PLR has, at this moment, three knights on the field; Saltgale has the crown). The phalanx splits the line. Saltgale is, for the second time in the match, knocked off the crown — this time by Roundeye, who has been waiting for this exact engagement angle for, by his post-match recount, "the entire match." Trashbright picks up the crown.</p>
        <p>14:18 — Score PLR 47 RCC 47. Trashbright is, at this moment, the most-attended-to knight in the venue. PLR's three remaining line knights converge on him. RCC's other four knights form a defensive ring around him. The crown ticks up.</p>
        <p>14:22 — Score PLR 47 RCC 48. The defensive ring holds. PLR's line takes one knight down (Coldcoat, by Trash) and is now two-on-five at the crown.</p>
        <p>14:28 — Score PLR 47 RCC 50. RCC wins. The Wave Doctrine's second sanctioned application produces the second consecutive comeback in Crown match — both matches the trailing team won, in both cases via wave-formation re-entry and sustained late-match crown contest.</p>
        <p>14:38 — Match over. The Polar Bear bench is silent. The Raccoon bench is, in the broadcast booth's mic, audibly cheering. Whitepaw the Steady, captain of PLR, walks to Trashbright at the post-match line and shakes his paw. Whitepaw says, on the open mic: <em>"You came up the hill together. We had won the hill four times. The hill is, today, yours. We will see you next bracket."</em> Trashbright nods. The post-match interview is brief. The Caucus's tactical analyst Pell Whittlestone, on the broadcast feed, calls the match <em>"the second confirmation of the doctrine's intended effect; we have, in two matches, seen the snowball not snowball; we will, I expect, see this become the new shape of Crown."</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— LMG broadcast transcript · Year 36 R2 Crown · RCC vs PLR · expanded into formal match record per Caucus archival request</div>

      <article class="log">
        <h3>Match Log: Year 36 R7, BDG vs MOS (Cleveland Boulder Pitch — the Wide Draw debut)</h3>
        <div class="meta">Official sportscaster transcript · 21:14 game time · the first sanctioned use of the Badgers' Wide Draw tactic · the post-match Caucus tactical-archive entry that has, by Featherquill's read, "ended the era in which Tank teams played slowly because they had to"</div>
        <p>00:00 — Match opens. Best-of-Five deathmatch on the Cleveland Boulder Pitch, the Badgers' home venue. Teams: Cleveland Boulder Badgers (BDG, all five active line returning) versus Saint-Laurent Antlerlords (MOS, founding-bell roster, Théodred Brisefer III "L'Ancrage" anchoring center). Pre-match consensus, by every analyst's read: a slow, grindy match. Both teams favor stationary tactics. The over-under on round length is set at six minutes and ten seconds.</p>
        <p>00:42 — Round 1. Antlerlords open in their standard L'Ancrage formation: Théodred III at center pitch, motionless; the four perimeter knights in concentric arcs, rotating clockwise around him at a measured walking pace. Badgers open in a four-knight floor-hold at the south end of the pitch with their fifth knight (the line's Sniper, Quartzbreaker) holding the high ground in the eastern catwalk. Standard Badger opening. The booth's commentators settle in for the expected slow round.</p>
        <p>01:38 — Round 1, 56 seconds in. Badger Tank Stoneflank breaks formation. He does not advance toward the L'Ancrage. He drifts west along the pitch's perimeter, in the slow loping gait the Coyotes call <em>la borradura</em>. The Antlerlords' rotating arc adjusts to track him; the rotation widens slightly to maintain the same arc-radius around the now-displaced threat. The booth's commentator, watching this, says on the broadcast: <em>"That is a Coyote tactic. The Badgers do not run the Coyote tactic. We are watching, by my read, a thing the Badgers are not supposed to be doing."</em> The commentator's read is wrong. The Badgers are doing this on purpose. The Antlerlords' coaching staff has not, at this moment, identified the tactic.</p>
        <p>01:55 — Round 1, second drift. Badger Brawler Coalfist drifts east. The Antlerlords' rotating arc now has two displaced threats and is, by the rotation's geometry, beginning to spread. L'Ancrage, at the center, does not move. The two Antlerlord knights still in the standard rotation are now twenty paces from the center on either side; the two displaced Antlerlord knights tracking the drifters are now thirty paces from center, at the perimeter, in an arc Théodred III cannot, by sight line, support without rotating his stance.</p>
        <p>02:18 — The wide draw closes. Both Badger drifters, on a coordinated signal from the bench (the bench used a small bell, audible on the LMG sideline mic; the Antlerlords' coaching staff has, in their post-match write-up, formally requested the Caucus investigate whether the bell counts as in-game communication; the Caucus has, in its preliminary response, declined to investigate), reverse direction simultaneously. The Antlerlord knights tracking the drifters are now caught in mid-perimeter, twenty paces from the L'Ancrage, with no cover. The Badger Sniper Quartzbreaker, on the catwalk, takes both Antlerlord perimeter knights in two shots over four seconds. Score: BDG 2 MOS 0 in active line. The Antlerlords now have two perimeter knights and L'Ancrage. The Badgers have all five.</p>
        <p>02:34 — The Antlerlords' coaching staff calls a tactical pause (a thirty-second mid-round pause permitted under Year-36 rules for major formation breakdowns). Théodred III is told, on the bench-to-pitch comm, to abandon the L'Ancrage stance and join the perimeter rotation as a fifth knight. The order is, by Antlerlord historical record, the first time L'Ancrage has been ordered off-anchor in a sanctioned match. Théodred III complies, slowly, in the way of his species. The Badgers, watching this on the field, do not press while the Antlerlord rotation reforms. They wait. The booth's commentator, watching the wait, says: <em>"That is — that is, frankly, sportsmanship. The Badgers are letting the Antlerlords reform. They could be pressing. They are not. The Badger coaching staff is, by every account I have ever heard, the most ruthless in the League. We are watching a thing I did not, in my career, expect to ever watch."</em> The commentator's read, here, is also wrong. The Badgers are not letting the Antlerlords reform out of sportsmanship. They are letting the Antlerlords reform because they have, in pre-match scouting, determined that the Antlerlords' five-knight perimeter rotation (without L'Ancrage at center) is, by tactical analysis, weaker than the four-plus-one rotation. The Badgers want the Antlerlords in the weaker formation. They are letting the Antlerlords get there.</p>
        <p>03:42 — Round 1 resumes. The Antlerlords' new five-knight perimeter rotation is, in execution, exactly as compromised as the Badger pre-match scouting predicted. Théodred III, in motion for the first time in the match, is the slowest knight in the rotation by a wide margin (he is, by the Caucus's mass register, the heaviest knight in the League; the rotation's pacing assumes a walking speed L'Ancrage cannot sustain). The rotation drags. The Antlerlords' coaching staff, watching the drag, calls another tactical pause to substitute Théodred out for a backup Tank. The Badgers, again, do not press. The substitution is made. The Antlerlords' new rotation, with the backup Tank in L'Ancrage's slot, is faster but lacks the gravitational mass — the new Tank cannot, by his own weight, hold the center. The rotation now has a center that drifts. The Badgers know this. The Badgers have been preparing for this for nine weeks of pre-season camp.</p>
        <p>04:18 — The Badgers' line advances, for the first time in the match, in a coordinated push. The push is the team's standard four-knight floor-hold, advancing one stride at a time, with the Sniper still on the catwalk providing covering fire. The Antlerlords' drifting center cannot, by formation geometry, repel a wall advance. The wall arrives. The Antlerlords lose two more knights in the engagement. Round 1 final: BDG 5 MOS 1 active. The Antlerlords have one knight standing — their captain, Marc-Olivier Brisefer, who at this point is in slow retreat toward the bench. He is permitted to walk off. The round resolves at 4:51 game time. Round 1 took, by stopwatch, three minutes and twenty-three seconds. The pre-match over-under was wrong by two minutes and forty-seven seconds.</p>
        <p>(Rounds 2 through 4 are reproduced in the official transcript and abbreviated here for archive.)</p>
        <p>16:38 — Round 4 closes. Score: BDG 3 MOS 1. The Badgers are one round away from the match. The Antlerlords have, across rounds 2 through 4, attempted three separate counter-tactics to the wide draw. The third counter — putting Théodred III in motion full-time as a roving anchor rather than a stationary one — was, by the LMG kinetics tracker's read, the closest the Antlerlords have come to a sustainable response. The roving anchor is, by every Caucus analyst's pre-existing tactical literature, an experimental formation. The Antlerlords had not, by their own coaching staff's frank admission, drilled it before this match. They drilled it in real time, in front of forty thousand spectators, on the most important regular-season match of their inaugural League run. The drill went, by the line's morale read, "fine, but not better than fine. We need eight more weeks of camp on this, and we have, instead, the Year 36 R8 schedule. We will be drilling it on the road."</p>
        <p>20:45 — Round 5 opens. The Antlerlords open with the roving anchor. The Badgers open in a five-knight floor-hold (the standard formation, no wide draw). The Antlerlords have, by visible bench instruction, decided to fight the match the Antlerlords' way and accept the loss if the loss comes. The Badgers — who have, by Slatebrush's pre-match commitment, drilled the wide draw for nine weeks — have, in this round, decided to give the Antlerlords the courtesy of a Tank-on-Tank match. The crowd notices. The crowd is, by the broadcast booth's read, completely silent. They have been watching tactical innovation for twenty minutes. They are now watching, in round 5, two Tank teams playing each other Tank-style. The crowd has not, in fifteen years of Cleveland home games, seen this kind of round.</p>
        <p>21:08 — Round 5, 23 seconds in. Théodred III, in his roving-anchor stance, walks directly toward Stoneflank. Stoneflank walks directly toward Théodred III. They meet at center pitch. They engage. The engagement is, by the kinetics tracker's read, a six-second exchange of plate-on-plate impacts that produces, on the official damage register, exactly equal damage to both Tanks. Stoneflank, who by archetype has slightly higher base HP, survives by a margin of one balloon. Théodred III is downed. The crowd erupts.</p>
        <p>21:14 — The Antlerlords' remaining four knights, watching their captain go down to a clean Tank engagement, do something the LMG broadcast booth has, in eight years of coverage, never seen. They walk forward in a single line. They engage the Badger line head-on. They do not rotate. They do not anchor. They fight. The round ends in a four-on-four melee that takes ninety seconds to resolve. The Badgers win, 4-1, on the strength of the Sniper still on the catwalk. The match resolves. Final: BDG 4 MOS 1.</p>
        <p>22:55 — Post-match line. Marc-Olivier Brisefer walks to Slatebrush. They shake. Brisefer says (the LMG mic captures this in Saint-Laurent creole; Estelle Roiseau-Manchot translates): <em>"You drilled this. We did not. We will drill. We will see you in the off-season exhibition. The wide draw is a good tactic. I am, frankly, glad it was not the Coyotes who debuted it on us. I would have, in that case, been less gracious. The Badgers we expected. The wide draw we did not. The combination was unfair, and the unfairness was the work. Well played."</em> Slatebrush nods. Slatebrush does not, in this moment, attempt to translate the wide draw's origin. Slatebrush has been told, by the Badgers' line, to not in any post-match interview call it the drift. Slatebrush calls it, on the post-match interview tape, only <em>"a Cleveland tactic, drilled in pre-season."</em> The Caucus, watching the tape, does not press. Coach Reyes of CYT, watching the tape from the Sonora basin training facility, sends Slatebrush a single private letter that reads, in its entirety: <em>"Well drifted. — Reyes."</em> Slatebrush has the letter framed in his office. He has not shown it, by his own commitment, to anyone outside the team.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— LMG broadcast transcript · Year 36 R7 BDG vs MOS · Cleveland Boulder Pitch · expanded into formal match record at the Caucus's tactical archive request · the Wide Draw debut</div>

      <article class="musing">
        <h3>"On the Bow"</h3>
        <div class="meta">A musing · originally a fan letter, now widely cited</div>
        <p>The Wolves, after they kill, sometimes bow. This is not a rule. The Wolves did not always do this. The Wolves started doing this in Year 33, after the Final at Brewer's Reach, after the Healer.</p>
        <p>I do not think the Wolves are sorry. I think the Wolves think the dead are sacred. I think the Wolves are pack animals, and to a pack animal a fallen opponent is still part of the pattern of the pack. The bow is not an apology. The bow is an acknowledgment.</p>
        <p>This is why the bow has been adopted by no other team. The bow is wolf physics. It does not translate.</p>
        <p>I do not, however, think the Sharks should make fun of it.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— anonymous fan letter, reprinted in <em>The Long Bow</em>, vol. 2</div>
      </article>

      <article class="musing">
        <h3>"Why a Healer Wanders"</h3>
        <div class="meta">A musing · author: a former Healer who now writes for the Beaver paper</div>
        <p>People ask me, often, why I sometimes drifted across the field during my matches. They saw it on the broadcast. They thought it was poor coaching. It was not.</p>
        <p>A Healer's job is, technically, to heal the lowest-HP teammate. A Healer's actual job is to keep the team alive.</p>
        <p>Sometimes the lowest-HP teammate is a Tank, and the Tank is fine, because the Tank has plate. Sometimes the lowest-HP teammate is a Speedster, and the Speedster will not stay still long enough to be healed. Sometimes the lowest-HP teammate is in a position where, if I follow them, I will die. So I do not follow them. I follow someone else, or I drift toward the center to keep my options open. The drift is not laziness. The drift is patience.</p>
        <p>What I am trying to say is that a Healer who looks aimless is, in fact, doing the most thinking on the field. Snipers, please remember this. (You will not.)</p>
        <div class="signoff">— guest column, <em>The Lobster Reach Daily</em></div>
      </article>

      <article class="musing">
        <h3>"On the Long Marketing Group"</h3>
        <div class="meta">A musing · this is what the Beavers actually think · do not print</div>
        <p>The League is funded, in part, by an organization called the Long Marketing Group. They own the broadcast rights. Their slogan is "If it's not on LMG, it didn't happen."</p>
        <p>This is why some matches do not happen.</p>
        <p>I am writing this in confidence and you are not supposed to repeat it. The LMG decides which matches get coverage. The matches that do not get coverage are not in the standings. They are off the books. They are <em>training matches,</em> per the rule book. They are also, sometimes, real matches that the LMG simply chose not to broadcast, for reasons that are, you may imagine, not always good.</p>
        <p>The Sharks have lost three matches that were, on paper, training matches. The Beavers have won two of those. The standings do not reflect this. The standings reflect what the LMG broadcast.</p>
        <p>I am not saying we should burn down the LMG offices. I am saying that, if the LMG offices were to burn down accidentally, I would not personally call the fire engine on duty.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— anonymous, BVR coaching staff, "do not print"</div>
      </article>

      <article class="musing">
        <h3>"On the Wave"</h3>
        <div class="meta">A musing · author: a Healer who has spent six matches respawning under the new Wave Doctrine</div>
        <p>The Caucus, in the first founding-bell working session of Year 36, formalized a thing the League had been slowly drifting toward for three seasons. They called it the <em>Wave Doctrine</em>. The doctrine has one rule: <em>knights of a downed team return to the field together, as a wave, not separately, as individuals.</em> The doctrine applies to the continuous-mode tournaments — the Crown matches, the Capture-the-Pole brackets, the Tag fixtures. It does not apply to deathmatch, where rounds reset everyone at once anyway.</p>
        <p>Before the doctrine, when a Hedgehog Striker was knocked out in a Crown match, that Hedgehog Striker would return to the field five seconds later, alone. They would walk to the center alone. They would arrive alone. They would, frequently, die alone, because the opposing team's full five was at the center waiting for them. The numbers, as a Sniper would say, were not on their side. The match's score would tick up against them, because the opposing team's crown-bearer had nothing to discourage him from sitting on the crown for the full five seconds, and then the next five, and then the next.</p>
        <p>This is, in fact, what most Crown matches looked like. Once one team gathered a numerical lead, the lead snowballed. The trailing team's individual-return knights walked into a wall. The wall held. The wall scored. The match was, by minute three, decided.</p>
        <p>The doctrine fixes this. When a team is reduced below some threshold — the doctrine says <em>"a meaningful fraction of the active line"</em>, which the Caucus has clarified informally to mean <em>"more than one"</em> — the next return wave gathers <em>everyone</em>. The downed knights wait, together, on the bench. They return, together, in a single wave. They cross the spawn line as a unit, in formation, with the slowest knight given a brief sprint allowance so the wave does not stretch out into the same disorganized trickle the doctrine was meant to prevent.</p>
        <p>This is, on paper, a small adjustment. In practice it has changed the entire shape of a Crown match.</p>
        <p>I have, in the six Crown matches we have played under the doctrine, been part of three return waves. The first one was a four-knight wave: four of us walked back to the field at once, in a loose diamond, with our Brawler at the front and our Sniper at the rear. We crossed the spawn line within two seconds of each other. We arrived at the center within four seconds of each other. The opposing team, who had been comfortable on the crown, scattered. They had, by the moment we crossed center, seen four knights moving as one and recognized that the math had changed. They moved off the crown. They moved into cover. The crown went unattended for six seconds. Six points of score did not happen because of those six seconds. We took the match.</p>
        <p>I have read the working-session minutes. The Caucus discussed, at length, whether the wave-return was unfair to the team that had earned a numerical lead. The Caucus's answer, as recorded, was: <em>"the lead is earned by the kill. The score is earned by the crown. These are two different earnings. The Wave Doctrine does not deny the kill. The Wave Doctrine denies the snowball."</em> I think this is correct. I will not, however, pretend the Wolves are happy about it. The Wolves were the team that benefited most from the snowball. The Wolves know it. The Wolves are, at this writing, on the third draft of a tactical adjustment that does not require the snowball to be effective. They will figure it out. They are, in the way of pack hunters, patient.</p>
        <p>The thing I want to write down — the reason I am writing this at all — is what it feels like to be in a wave. It feels like nothing else in the League feels. The five of us, on the bench, watching the match continue without us, are not five separate knights waiting for our individual countdowns. We are <em>the wave</em>. We talk to each other. We coordinate. We pick our formation. The Brawler asks the Sniper which side to enter from. The Sniper picks. The Tank confirms. The Speedster, who is the slowest of us by Stat Card but the fastest in the wave today on the sprint allowance, agrees to the diamond. We are, on the bench, planning our return as a team.</p>
        <p>And then the bell rings, and we cross the line, and we are a team. We were always a team. The previous individual returns were lonely because they were lonely. The wave is not lonely. The wave is, by its construction, the antidote to lonely.</p>
        <p>I do not, in general, like rules changes. I am a Healer. Rules changes complicate my job. The Wave Doctrine has not complicated my job. The Wave Doctrine has, in fact, given me back something I did not realize I had been losing. I had been losing the team. The team, in the previous individual-return system, was four knights at the center plus one knight walking back from the spawn line, again, alone. The wave gives me back the five.</p>
        <p>The Caucus did not, in their working-session minutes, name what they were trying to recover. They named what they were trying to fix. I think they were trying to fix the same thing. I think they did not, in their formal language, have the words. I am writing this to give them the words.</p>
        <p>The Wolves, when they bow to a fallen opponent, are acknowledging the dead. The Wave Doctrine, when it returns a downed team together, is acknowledging the living. Both are acknowledgments. The League is, in this small way, becoming a sport that acknowledges. I have been waiting eight seasons to write that sentence. I am glad to be writing it now.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— a HED Healer, six matches into the Wave Doctrine · published in <em>The Bayou Reach Quarterly</em>, Year 36 founding-bell issue</div>
      </article>

      <article class="musing">
        <h3>"On the Vendor Who Has Not Moved"</h3>
        <div class="meta">A musing · author: a fan-club newsletter editor · printed in The Brewer's Reach Reader, Year 35 winter issue · widely reprinted</div>
        <p>The lobster vendor on Brewer's Reach Pitch's eastern boundary has been there since before the inaugural match. She was there when the pitch was being marked. She was there when the founding bell was being installed. She was there when the Foundation steward responsible for the pitch's electrical hookups asked her, in Year 28's sixth week of construction, whether she had a permit. She did not have a permit. The steward, by Foundation lore, looked at her, looked at the lobsters in her tank, looked back at her, and walked away without filing a permit complaint. The vendor has been there since.</p>
        <p>What I want to write down is that this is, in my view, the single most stable institution in the Float Knights League. The League has, in eight seasons, expanded twice (Year 35 closeout, Year 36 mid-season Continental Expansion), restructured its bracket three times, ratified two major rule changes (the Marshmallow Protocol in Year 34, the Wave Doctrine in Year 36), and introduced four new venues. The lobster vendor has been there for all of it. Her booth is the same booth. Her sign is the same sign. Her prices are the same prices.</p>
        <p>I have, in writing this, asked the Foundation's Concession Row office for the vendor's name. The Foundation's Concession Row office has, by polite letter, declined to provide it. The letter said: <em>"The vendor has, by long-standing tradition, not given her name to any Foundation officer. We have not pressed. The vendor is the lobster vendor. The lobster vendor is the vendor. This is the relationship the Foundation has with the booth and we are, frankly, not going to ruin a good thing."</em> The letter was signed only with the Foundation's seal. I appreciated this. I will not, in this column, attempt to find out the vendor's name.</p>
        <p>What I will write is what I have been told, by a steward who would like to remain unnamed, about the vendor's prices. The vendor's prices have not changed since the inaugural match. A single lobster — large, fresh, prepared, with the small wax cup of melted butter — costs one bit. The Foundation's official concession-stand pricing has, in the eight intervening seasons, raised the equivalent item to four bits, six bits, and (in the Year 35 inflation adjustment) eight bits. The vendor's price has stayed at one bit. The Foundation has, on three occasions, requested that she raise her prices to match the official scale, on the grounds that her undercutting is bad for the Foundation's other vendors. The vendor has, on each occasion, replied with a single short letter that the Foundation has not, by its own decision, archived. The replies are, by the steward's account, identical: <em>"My lobster costs one bit. The price will not change. I will continue to operate the booth. If the Foundation wishes to close the booth, the Foundation may attempt to close the booth. I do not advise this. The booth is my booth and I will continue to sell lobster from it. With respect, the Foundation should consider its own pricing problems before it considers mine."</em></p>
        <p>The Foundation has, on each occasion, declined to close the booth.</p>
        <p>What this tells me is that the vendor is not, in any normal sense, operating a business. She is operating a presence. The lobster is the vehicle for the presence. The presence is what people come for. People come for the lobster, but they stay because the vendor is there. The vendor is, by my count, the longest-serving institution in the entire Float Knights organization — older than the Commissioner, older than the LMG broadcast booth, older than Pell Whittlestone's Foundry, older than the founding match itself. The League has, in its eight seasons, built itself around her. She has not moved.</p>
        <p>I went to the booth last week, on a non-match-day, and bought a lobster. The vendor, who was alone (she has never, in any account I have heard, employed a helper), prepared the lobster, handed me the wax cup, took my one bit, and said: <em>"Enjoy. The pitch is cleaner this morning than it has been in a fortnight. The cleaning crew is doing better. You should tell them. They do not, in general, get told."</em> I told the cleaning crew on my way out. They had not, in general, been told. They thanked me, awkwardly, in the way people thank you for something you have only delivered. I delivered the message. The vendor told me to. The vendor, by the cleaning crew's foreman's account, has done this before — she sees the work, she names the work, she tells someone to tell the workers. The workers do not, by tradition, ever know the message came from her. She has, by the foreman's read, no reason to do this. She does it.</p>
        <p>This is, I think, what stability looks like. Not as a structure. Not as a rule. Not as a building or a contract. Stability is a creature who has decided, against all economic logic, to be in one place forever, selling one thing at one price, and noticing the people around her who are doing their work well, and naming them so they get named. The League is built on her. The League knows it is built on her. The League will, when she is finally not at the booth one day, not know what to do with itself. I do not, on the day she is gone, want to be the columnist who has to write the column. I am writing this column instead, while she is still at the booth, so that, in the inevitable event, the column has been written. I am writing it down because she is real and present and one bit per lobster and the only thing in this entire sport that has not, in eight seasons, asked anyone to be patient with change.</p>
        <p>Buy a lobster from her. Tell the cleaning crew their work is clean. The vendor will not ask you to do this. She will be very glad you did.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— editorial column, <em>The Brewer's Reach Reader</em>, Year 35 winter issue · reprinted in nine subsequent fan publications, by editorial agreement</div>
      </article>

      <article class="musing">
        <h3>"Concerning the Float Gas Tasters"</h3>
        <div class="meta">A musing · by someone who claims they were one</div>
        <p>I have been a Float Gas taster for the Boise Brawling Badgers for nine seasons. I am not a Badger. I will not say what I am. The Foundry pays me in cured salmon, twice a month, dropped at my back door in a box that does not have a return address.</p>
        <p>I taste each batch of Float Gas before it ships. I have tasted a lot of Float Gas. Float Gas tastes like cold pennies and a quiet song you used to know. Sometimes the song changes. When the song changes, I do not approve the batch. The Foundry then redoes the batch.</p>
        <p>I do not know what the song means. I do know that, in Year 33, the song stopped, and the Foundry shut down, and the song came back, and the Foundry resumed. I do not have a theory about why. The Foundry has a theory. The Foundry has not shared it with me.</p>
        <p>I am writing this because someone should know. If I die in the next year, please tell my dog. The salmon is for the dog. The dog has a name. The Foundry knows it.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— anonymous, salmon delivery #2117</div>
      </article>

      <article class="musing">
        <h3>"On Permadeath"</h3>
        <div class="meta">A musing · by Coach Brask Ironclaw II, in the year of his son's death</div>
        <p>I lost my son this season. Brask the Third walked onto the field at Phoenix in Round 4 and did not walk off. He had three balloons. He used the third one finishing what he started. The League's report calls it "engagement complete." His mother and I call it Tuesday.</p>
        <p>I do not have a moral to share. People keep asking me what I have learned. I have learned nothing useful. I have learned that the League keeps every knight's helmet in a glass case in the Hall, and Brask's helmet is on a shelf next to his grandfather's, and the helmets <em>look the same</em>. I have learned that the Float Foundation will pay you for your kid in monthly installments and the installments are, in some technical sense, fair. I have learned that the Foxes have already drafted Brask's replacement.</p>
        <p>I have learned that the universe does not care that the Ironclaw line ended last Tuesday. The universe has a lot to do.</p>
        <p>I have not learned to forgive the Wolves. The Wolves did not kill him. The Wolves killed him three matches earlier in his career and he came back. I am going to spend the rest of my career not forgiving them anyway. The Wolves have offered to bow. They can keep their bow.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Brask Ironclaw II, FOX coaching staff, retirement letter</div>
      </article>

      <article class="musing">
        <h3>On Lobster</h3>
        <div class="meta">A musing · concession-row gossip · Boston, Brewer's Reach, ongoing</div>
        <p>The lobster vendor has been at Brewer's Reach since before the inaugural match. This is documented. There are photographs of the field on Match Day One, and the lobster booth is in them, already weathered, with a sign already missing the same letter (an "S," from "STEAMED"). The booth has not moved since. The vendor has not changed. She is older than every Beaver currently on roster. She is older than the Commissioner. She is, by some accounts, older than the founding paperwork.</p>
        <p>Foundation Day — the annual celebration of the inaugural match — is the only date the lobster vendor leaves Brewer's Reach. She catered the first Foundation Day in Year 29 (apparently as a personal gesture; the LMG had not yet incorporated and had not yet asked her). She has catered every Foundation Day since. She returns the morning after, at the same hour, in the same coat, with no luggage. Where she stays during her single night away is a topic of recurring concession-row debate. The leading theories are: (a) Helena, but no one in Helena has ever seen her; (b) underwater with the Otters, but the Otters have never confirmed; (c) she does not stay anywhere — she walks the night out and arrives the morning after on foot. Theory (c) does not explain how she gets to League Foundation Hall in the first place.</p>
        <p>The Float Foundation pays its larger settlements in lobster. This is widely understood as a quirk of the Foundation's accounting and dismissed as eccentric. The Foundation receives its lobster from one supplier. The supplier is the Brewer's Reach vendor. The Foundation has no other lobster source. The Foundation's bookkeepers have, on three occasions, attempted to acquire a backup supplier; on three occasions the backup supplier has been found to have closed shop the next morning, with no explanation, and the lobsters in the secondary fridge spoiled overnight. The Foundation has stopped trying.</p>
        <p>The vendor's prices have not changed since Year 28. Three coppers for a lobster roll. Five for a steamed pair. Lobster bisque is "available, ask," which has meant, in practice, that you have to be somebody to get the bisque. Bristlebeard the First got the bisque. Bristlebeard the Second did not. The Commissioner gets the bisque. The Beavers' current Tank does not. Crash Wartooth, on his last visit to Boston, was offered the bisque without asking; he declined politely. He was killed three matches later. Beavers fans who track these things consider the bisque a death omen. The Wolves do not.</p>
        <p>Some fans believe the lobster vendor is immortal. Some fans are correct.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Concession-Row Gazette, columns 1 through 47, condensed</div>
      </article>

      <article class="musing">
        <h3>On the First Sixty Seconds</h3>
        <div class="meta">A musing · The Wing Standard, Quarterly, Year 35 follow-up column</div>
        <p>A month after the field-widening, I am writing this from a press box at the Reno Open Court. Below me, two teams are walking forward across a brown court that is now, by Rules Committee fiat, three hundred and twenty units wider than it was at the start of the season. The two teams have not yet engaged. Neither has yet fired a shot. They are walking. The crowd is, by my count, leaned forward.</p>
        <p>The first sixty seconds of every round used to be the dullest part of a Float Knights match. The Snipers fired. The Brawlers ran. The Healers crouched. By the thirty-second mark, two or three knights were already wounded, and the round's eventual shape was already drawn. The middle of the round was the best part. The first minute was filler. Coaches, in the off-season, have privately admitted as much.</p>
        <p>The wider field has rewritten this. The first sixty seconds are now the part of the round in which nothing has happened yet but everything is being decided. Where you put your Tank in the opening forty seconds determines whether your Sniper has a clean line at the eighty-second mark. Where you put your Healer in the opening twenty seconds determines whether you have a Healer at the ninety-second mark. The Brawlers, who used to charge straight at the center, now have to choose a lane. The Speedsters, who used to flank with reckless abandon, now have to time the flank. The decisions have not gotten harder. The decisions have gotten visible.</p>
        <p>I do not know if the crowd is leaning forward because the opening minute is now interesting, or because they have been told the opening minute is now interesting and are watching to confirm. Both are valid. The result is the same: the bleachers are quieter than they used to be, and the quiet is the kind that means people are paying attention.</p>
        <p>Below me, the Brawlers reach the center line. The Healers settle into position behind their Tanks. The first shot of the round goes off — a Sniper in red, fifty yards out, into a Healer's left flank. The wounded Healer does not retreat. They stand their ground and spend the round patching the teammates around them, taking three more hits, and dying with one balloon left at the seventy-second mark. The Sniper's team loses the round at the second-twenty-eight mark by failing to break the wounded line.</p>
        <p>The crowd is still leaning forward. They are louder now. The opening minute has stopped being filler.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Talia Featherquill, "The Bleachers Are Quiet," Wing Standard Quarterly, Year 35</div>
      </article>

      <article class="musing">
        <h3>The Healer's Creed</h3>
        <div class="meta">A musing · attributed to Dr. Lopecora Plumstone (HED Healer, founding generation) · Year 31, retransmitted</div>
        <p>I do not heal because I am kind. I heal because the alternative is unbearable. There is a difference, and the difference matters.</p>
        <p>A kind Healer would patch the knights they like and leave the knights they do not. A kind Healer would, in a hard moment, hesitate. A kind Healer would, watching a wounded enemy bleed out at the corner, let them. I have seen Healers like this. They retire early. They are not, by the time they retire, very kind anymore. The job has eaten the kindness out of them and left a careful, frightened person who cannot any longer tell whether they are doing right.</p>
        <p>I heal because I cannot watch a balloon pop. This is not metaphorical. I cannot watch the small hiss and the small slump and the small stillness afterward. The first time I watched it happen on the field — and it was a Wolf, in fact, an enemy, although I did not know yet that we had enemies — I walked from my position to theirs and patched them up before the round resolved. The Wolves complained. The League fined me. The League also, after some debate, codified the role I had just invented. I was, in that order: a Brawler with poor judgment, a problem, a precedent, a job description.</p>
        <p>The job description has gotten more refined since Year 28. Healers now know what they are. We are not Brawlers with poor judgment. We are the knights who walk toward the knights who are about to die, and we patch the leak before the hiss starts. We do this for our team. We do this for our enemies, when we can. We do this because the alternative — watching, doing nothing, kindly — is the worst version of being on the field.</p>
        <p>Train your Healers well. Pay them what you can. Do not ask them, in the locker room, whether they enjoy the job. They do not. They do it because the alternative is unbearable. That is the only reason that holds up under fire.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Dr. Lopecora Plumstone, "Notes Toward a Healer's Manual," Year 31 · republished by the Healers' Mutual Aid Society, Year 35</div>
      </article>
    </div>
    </div>

      <article class="found">
        <h3>Letter from the south · postmarked Lima, delivered Year 35 to the Yucatan League outpost</h3>
        <div class="meta">Found Paper · two-page letter, formal Spanish · the writer has identified themselves only as "a representative of the basin coordinating council" · the letter has been translated by Estelle Roiseau-Manchot at the Foundation's request</div>
        <p>Translated text, with formal Spanish formality preserved where it survives translation:</p>
        <p><em>"To the Yucatan League outpost, with greetings,</em></p>
        <p><em>The basin coordinating council has, in receipt of your Year 34 inquiry regarding southern continental participation in the Float Knights League, deliberated for two seasons. The deliberation has, regrettably, not produced an affirmative response. The reasons follow.</em></p>
        <p><em>The southern animal communities — comprising, by our register, twenty-three settled lizard-line communities, eleven alligator-line communities, fourteen serpentine-line communities, and an indeterminate number of tropical bird communities (the bird communities do not, by their own preference, register their numbers; we have estimated forty, but the estimate is, by every honest reading, low) — have, on consultation, declined to send delegations northward. The reasons are three.</em></p>
        <p><em>First: travel distance. The continent's central rail does not connect south of the Yucatan extension, and our communities are not, in the aggregate, willing to fund a connecting line. The funding shortfall is structural, not ideological. We have not the surplus.</em></p>
        <p><em>Second: predator-prey unease. The northern League has, by our review of your existing roster, several teams whose species lines are predator species in our jungle ecology — the Foxes, the Wolves, the Lynx, and the Sharks all register as threats to specific southern lines. Our serpentine communities, in particular, have indicated that they would not, in good conscience, send athletes into a venue where they would be required to share a locker tunnel with a Lynx. The unease is not, by our read, irrational. The Lynx have not, by your own League's record, eliminated the predator instinct from their working lives. We do not blame them. We do not, however, ask our communities to room with them.</em></p>
        <p><em>Third: climate adaptation. Our jungle communities are not, by physiology, suited to the venues your League routinely plays in. The Helena Glacier Rink would, by every honest assessment, be lethal to a basin lizard within forty minutes of arrival. We do not have a counter-proposal that would shift your venue rotation to accommodate us; we recognize that your continental venue distribution is the venue distribution and that we are asking for a substantial accommodation if we ask it.</em></p>
        <p><em>We thank you, formally, for the inquiry. We extend, equally formally, an invitation: should the League ever wish to play exhibition matches at one of our southern venues — the Lima Highlands Pitch, the Caracas Canopy Hall, the Buenos Aires Wetlands — we will host. The hosting will be hospitable. The hosting will not, on our part, include the dispatching of teams northward in return. We hope this is acceptable. We hope, in any case, that the Float Knights League prospers in its current form, and we will, with respectful interest, follow it from here.</em></p>
        <p><em>With respect,</em><br/>
        <em>— a representative of the basin coordinating council, by signature redacted at the council's request"</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— Yucatan League outpost · letter file Year 35 · translated by Estelle Roiseau-Manchot, fee paid in clams · Foundation has not, formally, responded</div>
      </article>

The first coach was — the Lynx pronoun used here is not 'I' or 'we' and has, by Roiseau-Manchot, no neutral League-Common rendering — and the second coach was, in the same fashion, untranslatable. The 4 bits, by Foundation calculation, would have returned 24. Whether the bettor returned to claim the payout is unrecorded. The slip's torn front means the bet ID cannot be matched to the Cup's payout register.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Foundation Ephemera Drawer · betting-slip back fragment Year 36 · the slip's payout, if claimed, was claimed without the slip</div>
      </article>

      <article class="found">
        <h3>Crowd graffiti · Helena Glacier Rink stairwell, level 2 · accumulated Years 35-36 · transcribed in chronological order of additions</h3>
        <div class="meta">Found Paper · pencil and pen, multiple hands, the wall has not been repainted since the Quillstrike record · transcription performed weekly by the venue's evening cleaner, who has saved every iteration</div>
        <p>The wall, in chronological order of additions (the cleaner has dated each line by the night they noticed it):</p>
        <p><em>(Year 35 R3, the night of the 412-pace mark)</em>: <em>"412. the longest line ever drawn."</em></p>
        <p><em>(Year 35 R3, two hours later, different hand)</em>: <em>"and the shooter is gone."</em></p>
        <p><em>(Year 35 R3, dawn, a third hand)</em>: <em>"the line is not gone. the line stays."</em></p>
        <p><em>(Year 35 R8, the night Sundip tied the mark)</em>: <em>"the line was tied. the line is now two lines. the lines stay."</em></p>
        <p><em>(Year 35 R8, two hours later)</em>: <em>"and now the second shooter is gone too."</em></p>
        <p><em>(Year 35 R8, the next morning)</em>: <em>"the lines stay. the shooters do not. the lines remember the shooters. — a Helena fan, no team affiliation"</em></p>
        <p><em>(Year 36 founding bell, the day Hester Quillstrike's twin took the field for the first time wearing Hester's old number)</em>: <em>"the lines stay. the third shooter is on the field. the third shooter is the first shooter's twin. the lines are watching."</em></p>
        <p><em>(Year 36 R3, after the twin's first sanctioned kill)</em>: <em>"a new line. shorter than 412. it counts anyway."</em></p>
        <p><em>(Year 36 R6, after the twin's first long-distance shot — 287 paces, well short of the mark)</em>: <em>"the twin is the twin. the twin is not the sister. the line is its own line. — H., a Helena fan, sister to a different shooter (yes). i hope the twin understands."</em></p>
        <p>The wall has not been repainted. The Helena venue's coaching staff has issued a standing instruction that it be left as-is. The cleaner has been told that her weekly transcription is, by the staff's read, the official record. She has, in private, told the Foundation Drawer's curator that she has been adding her own line each week — in pencil, very small, in the bottom corner — and has not, in any of her transcriptions, included her own additions. <em>"They are not for the public,"</em> she said. <em>"They are for the wall. The wall knows what I have written."</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— Helena Glacier Rink stairwell, level 2 · cleaner's chronological transcription Years 35-36 · the cleaner's own additions are not transcribed and are, by her instruction, never to be</div>
      </article>

      <article class="found">
        <h3>Postcard · Reno postmark · Year 36 R7 day-after · sent to Coach Reyes, Sonora basin training facility</h3>
        <div class="meta">Found Paper · single picture postcard, generic Reno-Strip souvenir, addressed in block lettering · the front shows a tourist photograph of the Reno Open Court at night · the back has the postage and the message · the writing is in a hand the Coyotes' bench staff has identified as belonging to a Cleveland Boulder Pitch parking-lot attendant</div>
        <p>Front: a generic Reno-Strip tourist postcard. The Open Court at night, the brass crown's silhouette on the stadium's banner.</p>
        <p>Back, block lettering: <em>"Coach Reyes — the Cleveland parking lot attendant has, by long-standing personal practice, watched every Badger home match for the past nine seasons. This evening's match was, by my honest assessment, the strangest single match I have witnessed in nine years. I do not understand the wide draw. I do not need to. The post-match parking-lot conversations were, however, unanimous: every Badger fan who came past my booth, on their way out, said some variation of 'we did the Coyote thing tonight.' I have never, in nine seasons, heard any team's fans describe their team's tactic by another team's name. This is, by my read, an unusual evening. I thought you would want to know. — a Cleveland parking-lot attendant, no team affiliation, just a witness."</em></p>
        <p>The postcard is, by the Coyotes' team facility's display archive, the document that has become known as <em>"the well-drifted card"</em> — the same item referenced in the Lore tab's Coyotes entry. The original is on a wall in the Sonora training facility, framed, signed by Coach Reyes himself with the single word <em>"received."</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— Foundation Ephemera Drawer · postcard duplicate · the original is in the Coyotes' Sonora facility · the parking-lot attendant has not, by Foundation knowledge, been formally thanked</div>
      </article>

      <article class="found">
        <h3>Children's drawing, second submission · Boston Foundation Hall lobby corkboard · Year 36 founding bell</h3>
        <div class="meta">Found Paper · crayon and marker on construction paper, approximately 12 inches by 18 inches · signed by "ELLE" with a small heart and the addition "(I AM TEN NOW)" · pinned next to the original Year 35 carry drawing</div>
        <p>The drawing, by the Foundation lobby steward's description: <em>"a single figure in plate, in the Boise Brawling Badger team colors (brown and gold), standing in a circle of smaller figures who are, by my read, four other Badgers and a coach. The figure in the center has a label arrow pointing to him reading 'STONEFLANK.' The smaller figures have label arrows that read, in order, 'COALFIST,' 'QUARTZBREAKER,' 'TWO MORE BADGERS,' and 'COACH SLATEBRUSH WHO IS NICE.' Below the central figure, in block letters, the caption reads: 'THE WIDE DRAW WORKED. WELL DRIFTED. — ELLE, age 10.'"</em></p>
        <p>The drawing was submitted by mail to the Foundation Hall's general-correspondence box with a short note in the same hand: <em>"i drew the wolves carrying the healer when i was 9. i am 10 now. the badgers won with the wide draw and i wanted to draw it. you can put it next to the other one. — Elle."</em> The Foundation lobby steward, on receipt, pinned it to the corkboard next to the Year 35 Greylane drawing. Both drawings are now, by Foundation tradition, permanent installations on the corkboard. The corkboard's center two pins are reserved, in perpetuity, for ELLE's contributions.</p>
        <p>Coach Slatebrush has, on his next Foundation visit, been informed that he is described in a child's drawing as "nice." His response, per the Foundation steward's note: <em>"He looked at it for a long time. He did not say anything. He took out his notebook. He wrote down 'nice.' He put the notebook away. He went to lunch. He did not, before leaving, comment on the drawing. The drawing is still on the corkboard."</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— Foundation Hall lobby corkboard · ELLE's second submission · Year 36 founding bell · permanent installation, Foundation tradition</div>
      </article>

      <article class="found">
        <h3>Locker-room scribble · Sonora Coyote training facility · marker on the inside of locker 6 · Year 36, post-R7</h3>
        <div class="meta">Found Paper · permanent marker on the inside of locker 6's door, behind the team gear · noticed by the team's equipment manager during off-season cleaning · transcribed before being left in place</div>
        <p>The scribble, in three lines, in a hand the Coyote bench staff has confirmed belongs to the Speedster who keeps the working journal:</p>
        <p><em>"the wide draw worked.</em><br/>
        <em>they did not call it the drift.</em><br/>
        <em>that is fine.</em><br/>
        <em>the work is the work. the name is the name. the work and the name do not, this season, need to be the same word."</em></p>
        <p>The equipment manager, on noticing the scribble, asked the Speedster whether to clean it off. The Speedster declined. The locker has, since, been left intact. The locker has also, by the Speedster's own quiet practice, been the locker assigned to her every season since she joined the team. She has, by team tradition, the right to leave whatever marks on the inside of the door she likes. The door is hers until she leaves the team.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Sonora Coyote training facility · locker 6, inside door · scribble Year 36 post-R7 · transcribed by team equipment manager, scribble retained in place</div>
