    <div class="lore-section" data-loresection="timeline">
      <article class="history">
        <h3>The League Timeline</h3>
        <div class="meta">A working chronology · Float Foundation Archive · entries drafted, in each instance, by whoever was on duty the week the event was filed</div>
        <p>The events below use League Years (LY), counted from the founding of the Boston Brisk Beavers and the inaugural match at Brewer's Reach. The Long Quiet — formerly called the Collapse, in older League documents — is in the unstated past, three to five centuries before the founding bell. The League's current season is Year 36. The chronology that follows is not exhaustive; we have written down what we could remember, and what the team archives would let us write down, and what the lobster vendor confirmed when we asked.</p>
        <div class="lore-timeline">
          <ol>
            <li><span class="yr">Pre-League</span><div class="ev">The continent reorganizes itself. Boston rallies around the workshop floor. Tampa rallies around the salvage tide. Reno rallies around the one slot-machine power line that, by Year 8 of the post-Long-Quiet calendar, has not stopped humming. The Hedgehogs of Helena have already been running backyard tournaments for three generations and pay no attention to anyone else's chronology. The lobster vendor takes up the booth at the Brewer's Reach pitch site three years before the pitch is built. She is asked, by the construction crew, whether she will move while they work. She says no. They build around her. She is still there.</div></li>
            <li><span class="yr">Year 28</span><div class="ev">The League is founded. The Boston Brisk Beavers play the inaugural match at Brewer's Reach Pitch against the Wichita Wild Wolves, a team that has been a team for six weeks. The Beavers win. Old Bristlebeard the First dies in the inaugural championship's final round, taking three opposing knights with him. His Riot Shield enters circulation as the League's first scavenged legacy item; it is the first object recorded in the lineage chain. The lobster vendor sells, by her own ledger, four hundred and twelve lobsters across the season. Her ledger no longer survives; the figure is from her granddaughter's recollection.</div></li>
            <li><span class="yr">Year 29</span><div class="ev">The Wolves win their first championship. Hardvein Quickstep, captain, accepts the trophy without comment, walks off the post-match line, and goes home. The pack does not, in any season since, celebrate publicly. The Bow ritual does not yet exist; the Wolves will not develop it for another four years.</div></li>
            <li><span class="yr">Year 30</span><div class="ev">The Tampa Tornado Sharks and the Boise Brawling Badgers join the League. The Boise Float Gas Foundry begins commercial production. Pell Whittlestone, the Foundry's chief chemist, ships a flat batch to Tampa. The Sharks use it anyway. They win their home opener 5-0 over the Foxes. The Foundry rewrites its outgoing-inspection protocol the next year. The exploit will not, by Whittlestone's quiet personal commitment, be available again. The disclosure of the incident waits until Year 33.</div></li>
            <li><span class="yr">Year 31</span><div class="ev">The Phoenix Furious Foxes and the Kansas Kicking Kits join. Commissioner Margaux Whiskerstone takes the office, which had been informally administered for three seasons by a rotating committee. Whiskerstone's first formal act is to sit on a contested deed for two weeks until both parties agree to a settlement; the deed is for the Reno Open Court. The settlement gives the Court to the Reno municipal authority, with a long-term League lease at a rate the lobster vendor would consider reasonable. The first Coronation Cup is held that summer. Whittlestone forges the brass crown in her off-season and bills the League for one lobster. The bill has not been paid. The Raccoons, who do not yet exist as a League team, win the inaugural Cup with a four-team round-robin appearance. The crown is reported missing the morning after. The Reno pawn shop is identified within twelve hours.</div></li>
            <li><span class="yr">Year 32</span><div class="ev">The Seattle Sleepless Owls and the Fresno Frantic Frogs join. Vela Hootington, OWL Speed in her inaugural season, dies on a 22-kill streak; the next two knights to attempt to break the streak die in the same round trying. Mira Pawington, eldest of the Kits' founding litter, dies completing her career as the Scavenger Queen with her opponent's Power Cell still in her hand. The Pawington Cup is named after her by the Commissioner that same season, while she is still on the active roster. Mira lives long enough to see the trophy. She does not see the second running of the Cup; she dies in Year 32 R7. The Cup is, by her surviving siblings' request, kept in their family's hayloft when not on display.</div></li>
            <li><span class="yr">Year 33</span><div class="ev">The Portland Punching Pandas and the Olympia Outlaw Otters join. The Foundry shuts down for forty-one days mid-season; no public explanation is given. A half-burned page from the Foundry break room, recovered after the shutdown ends, suggests there was a tank that smelled wrong, and that Whittlestone — who at this point had been chief chemist for five years — handled it without telling the League. The League does not, in the year that follows, ask. The Foundry resumes operations on day forty-two. The Badgers, who had been playing on reserve gas during the shutdown, finish 2-12 — the worst season of their tenure to date, before or since.</div></li>
            <li><span class="yr">Year 33 (continued)</span><div class="ev">The Brewer's Reach Final, Beavers versus Wolves. In round three Bristlebeard the Second's railgun shot, meant for Wolves' Striker Crash Wartooth, lands instead on Wolves' Healer Avery Loambright. Loambright dies before she hits the pitch. The Wolves win the round and the match and the championship. At the post-match line they form a circle around the chalk mark where Loambright fell, and Halfmoon Greylane bows for eleven seconds in the wolf way. The bow has been observed at every subsequent Wolves' pre-match Hall visit. It lasts, every time, eleven seconds. The duration was set on its first observation and has not, in any subsequent observance, varied.</div></li>
            <li><span class="yr">Year 33 (later)</span><div class="ev">Reef Tinkerbarrel, the retired Sharks' equipment manager, publishes the eighth installment of his serialized memoir in The Lobster Reach Daily. The eighth installment contains the full text of the Year 30 R3 Tampa flat-batch logbook. The Caucus convenes an emergency working session and votes 11-4 to let the Year 30 R3 result stand. The Sharks acknowledge the practice; the Sharks apologize publicly; the Foxes accept the apology publicly. Bristlebeard the First's Riot Shield is lost on the field at the season's final, en route to the vault, and the Reno Heist begins. The Beavers are still angry.</div></li>
            <li><span class="yr">Year 34</span><div class="ev">The Reno Rascal Raccoons join. They debut by winning the Year 34 Coronation Cup. The crown is reported missing the next morning; it is recovered by lunch at Quickfingers' shop, on Reno's South Strip, where it has been deposited overnight under a pawn ticket made out to the active Raccoon roster's captain. The Foundation creates a recurring annual budget line: <em>"crown retrieval logistics"</em>, four lobsters and a small storage fee, paid every year a Raccoon wins the Cup. Felix Marshmallow, PND Tank, is killed by friendly grenade fire mid-match; the Marshmallow Protocol is enacted league-wide and pre-season grenade-safety drills are made mandatory. Crash Wartooth is stunned three times in twelve seconds and survives the round but tears a knee tendon doing so; the Crash Rule is enacted, requiring all Wolves Brawlers to wear heavy plate. Wartooth recovers and returns the next season. He is still on the active line as of Year 36.</div></li>
            <li><span class="yr">Year 35</span><div class="ev">The Year 35 closeout expansion brings four new teams: the Helena Hidden Hedgehogs, the Bayou Tigers, the Anchorage Polar Bears, and the Pittsburgh Steelwing Ravens. The Polar Bears walked thirty-two days to petition for admission and were admitted on the strength of the petition's first sentence. Hester Quillstrike, HED Sniper, sets the longest-shot record in League history at the Helena Glacier Rink in HED's third match — four hundred and twelve paces along the diagonal of the rink. She dies in the same match. Sundip Hootington Jr., OWL Sniper, ties her record exactly later that same year at the Reno Open Court, climbing the Power Core to celebrate; the Core overloads and he does not survive. His shot also kills the Frog Speedster he had just shot, who had been wounded by Sundip's mark and was in the blast radius. The League patches the overload latency that off-season. The Rifle Hester carried first falls at the base of the Core and is scavenged in cleanup; it has been at large since.</div></li>
            <li><span class="yr">Year 35 (later)</span><div class="ev">Halfmoon Greylane, in the Year 35 quarterfinal at Olympia, carries downed Healer Pinedrift across forty-eight paces of open pitch under sustained Sniper fire. She takes fourteen hit registers and does not return fire during the carry. Pinedrift survives. The match playback is in the Caucus's archive under the file name <em>"Greylane carry — do not edit."</em> Greylane refuses to allow it as a training video. The Year 35 Coronation Cup goes to RCC for the sixth time. The crown is, again, reported missing the morning after. The Personal Sandbag enters the bettor's storefront. The Knights' Union petitions for a notification system. The Commissioner declines. The Wing Standard editorializes. The item remains for sale. The League's Ethics Committee files a formal opinion that the item is sabotage with a price tag. The opinion does not change policy. Both sides claim the moral high ground.</div></li>
            <li><span class="yr">Year 35 (closing)</span><div class="ev">The Reno Cultural Office paper Project Neon Inheritance leaks via a junior intern. The paper had been internal-only and described in detail how Reno's three-block lower-Strip survival was a direct consequence of one continuous slot-machine power line that survived the Long Quiet. The Cultural Office does not comment. The leak does not damage anyone. The League Library quietly accessions a copy. The Rules Committee announces a venue-floor expansion: arena dimensions are formally widened so that no Sniper can, from spawn, fire on a still-spawning opponent. The change is justified as restoring the tactical opening phase. The Wolves are unhappy. The Otters are euphoric. Featherquill writes a column. The League adapts.</div></li>
            <li><span class="yr">Year 36</span><div class="ev">The Continental Expansion brings four further teams in mid-season: the Whitehorse Lynx, the Saint-Laurent Antlerlords, the Sonora Drifting Coyotes, and the Yucatan Vibrant Quetzals. Théodred Brisefer III takes the L'Ancrage anchor position for the Antlerlords and, in the team's founding-bell debut against the Ravens at Boise, stands in the center of the pitch for nine minutes without swinging his antlers. The post-match nod produces the largest single-match viewer mailbag of the founding bell. The first Frostfall Friendly between the Polar Bears and the Lynx is played at the Boise Frosthold Pitch in pre-season; the Cold Stones trophy is established. The Caucus ratifies the Commitment Directive (a coaching standard against the dither) and the Wave Doctrine (the team-formation respawn rule) at the founding-bell working session. The Wave Doctrine produces, in its first two sanctioned applications, two consecutive comeback wins for the trailing team — the snowball, by Pell Whittlestone's broadcast call, has been broken.</div></li>
            <li><span class="yr">Current</span><div class="ev">The League continues. The Riot Shield is somewhere. The Foundry hums. The Wolves bow eleven seconds. The Healers wander when they need to. The Snipers, since Loambright, do not target Healers when any other knight is in range. The Float Foundation pays out in lobster, in installments, with crab and clam and crawfish and oyster on the side ledger by mutual agreement. The lobster vendor is still at her booth. Her prices have not changed. The Reno pawn-shop arrangement is in its sixth year. The Hall of Fallen Heroes has eight rows; six are full, the seventh has Loambright in it, the eighth is partially populated and growing slowly. The League has not, in eight years, found a way to be uncomplicated. It has, in eight years, found ways to be honest about the complications. This is a fair trade. The lobster is still one bit. The crowd has not stopped noticing.</div></li>
          </ol>
        </div>
      </article>
    </div>

    <!-- ===== GLOSSARY ===== -->
    <div class="lore-section" data-loresection="glossary">
      <article class="history lore-glossary">
        <h3>Glossary of Terms</h3>
        <div class="meta">Reference · maintained by the League Office Editorial Board</div>
        <dl>
          <dt>The 412-Pace Mark</dt>
          <dd>The League's longest single-shot kill on record, named for the LMG kinetics tracker's measurement of the firing distance — four hundred and twelve paces along the diagonal of the venue. Set by Hester Quillstrike, HED Sniper, at the Helena Glacier Rink in HED's inaugural season — the same shot was, in the moment of its making, the shot that took her life, by the coordinated four-Otter rush at the next round's open. Tied — exactly, never broken — by Sundip Hootington Jr., OWL Sniper, at the Reno Open Court later that same year, on a shot taken with the Rifle Hester had carried first. The mark is now jointly held, posthumously, by both shooters. The mark's measurement is contested, in colloquial usage, by a small but persistent Reno-academy faction that refers to it as "the 412-pixel mark" — a piece of slang that originated in a Year-36 graduate-thesis presentation in which the student, having spent six weeks in the Cultural Office's Old-Ones-screen archive, used the wrong word for the unit and was, mid-presentation, gently corrected by her advisor. The slang escaped the seminar room. The slang has not, in two seasons, escaped the Reno-academy. The Records Committee uses paces. The Foundation uses paces. The fans who care about the figure use paces. The slang exists. We are noting that it exists. We are, for clarity, calling it the 412-Pace Mark in this glossary. The slang is fine. The pace is the unit.</dd>

          <dt>The Balloon Contract</dt>
          <dd>The standard agreement signed by every Knight before joining a roster. Specifies that a Knight is allotted three balloons per match, popped one-per-knockout. The third pop ends the Knight's match (and, after enough cumulative pops across their career, ends the Knight). Allegedly proposed by Splinter Tooth in Year 28.</dd>

          <dt>The Bayou Walk</dt>
          <dd>The Tigers' pre-match ritual, first introduced at the Year 36 founding bell. The four Tiger knights of the active line walk the perimeter of the Bayou Cypress-Hollow venue once before the opening bell, in a single column, slowly, without speaking. The matriarch (Stripeshoulder, as of Year 36) walks at the front. The Walk is not, by the Tigers' own account, a strategic element. It is a way of greeting the field. The Tigers continue the practice at away matches when the host venue permits it; most do.</dd>

          <dt>The Bow</dt>
          <dd>A Wolf-pack ritual, first observed at Brewer's Reach in Year 33. After a fallen opponent goes down, the Wolves on the field briefly form a circle around the body and the captain bows. Not adopted by any other team. The Wolves themselves consider it a form of acknowledgment, not apology.</dd>

          <dt>The Old Ones</dt>
          <dd>The prior dominant species on this continent. Walked upright on two legs. Built the cities every animal community now lives in. Wrote the runes painted on every concrete wall, metal sign, and street pole. Have been gone, by the most careful Reno-academy dating, for between three and five centuries — the dating is contested but no scholar puts the Long Quiet at less than three hundred years ago. They lived alongside our great-great-great-grandparents at the most generous reading. Their physical artifacts (concrete, steel, glass, latex paint, foundry slag, the occasional intact dolly rig) persist where they were sheltered from rain. The League does not, formally, take a position on what the Old Ones were. Most animals do not, in daily life, think about them at all. Some scholars think about them more than is healthy.</dd>

          <dt>The Long Quiet</dt>
          <dd>The centuries-ago event when the prior dominant species (the Old Ones) ceased to be present. Estimated three to five hundred years before the League's founding; the dating is contested by perhaps a hundred years on either end. Whatever happened to them did not, as far as anyone has been able to determine, leave physical evidence beyond the absence itself. Their cities, runes, machines, and a great many of their tools remain. The League does not require any Knight to have an opinion on the Long Quiet to play. The League does, however, require that you do not vandalize Old-Ones ruins. Formerly called "the Collapse" in older League documents — the term remains in use informally, though the Long Quiet is now the formally preferred term per the Year-36 Pamphlet revision.</dd>

          <dt>Concession Row</dt>
          <dd>The strip of food vendors along the eastern boundary of Brewer's Reach Pitch, Boston. Notable for the lobster vendor who has been there since before the inaugural match (Year 28) and has not, for any reason, ever moved her booth. Her prices have not changed since the League's founding. She is the Float Foundation's sole lobster supplier.</dd>

          <dt>The Coronation Cup</dt>
          <dd>The League's annual single-match crown event, held at the Reno Open Court on Foundation Day. A brass crown (forged Year 32 by Pell Whittlestone of Boise) spawns at the center of the arena; whoever wears it scores team points per second but cannot fire a weapon. First team to fifty points wins. RCC has won six of eight. The crown has been reported "missing for inspection" the morning after every RCC win and recovered, every time, in a Reno pawn shop. The League's Atlas Committee has stopped commenting.</dd>

          <dt>The Denver Stand</dt>
          <dd>The Bison's home-match tradition: the patriarch (Yellowhide, as of Year 35) stands at the south end of the Highland-Plains pitch in full ceremonial harness for the duration of every home match. Not a coaching role. The herd-rotation tactical style requires every Bison knight to know where the herd's center of gravity is at all moments; Yellowhide is, by tradition, that gravity. Opposing teams have learned to orient on him too — by the third pre-League exhibition match, every visiting knight had unconsciously adjusted their positioning relative to his standing point.</dd>

          <dt>Crash Rule</dt>
          <dd>See <em>The Crash Rule</em>, further down. The bare name is the in-locker-room shorthand; the entry below has the full version with the named knight, the year, and Wartooth's later comment on it.</dd>

          <dt>Felix Drills</dt>
          <dd>See <em>The Felix Drills</em>, further down. The shorthand "Felix Drills" is the in-locker-room name; the formal Caucus name is <em>The Marshmallow Protocol's grenade-safety training</em>; the entry below uses the locker-room name as the headword on the grounds that, in eight seasons, no knight has ever, in the locker room, called it the Marshmallow Protocol's grenade-safety training.</dd>

          <dt>The Float Foundation</dt>
          <dd>A neutral non-profit jointly funded by the League and the LMG. Operates the Hall of Fallen Heroes, pays out benefits to surviving family of permadeath Knights (often in lobster, by family request), and runs the Foundation Hall venue for Foundation Day events.</dd>

          <dt>Float Gas</dt>
          <dd>The proprietary lifting gas that fills League-spec balloons. Distilled at the Boise Float Gas Foundry. Each team receives a different formula: Boise gets the heaviest batch (with regulators); Olympia gets the lightest; Phoenix gets the desert formula (high-altitude expansion); etc. Composition is patented and undisclosed. The Foundry shut down for 41 days in Year 33 with no explanation.</dd>

          <dt>The Float Gas Tasters</dt>
          <dd>A small group of (allegedly non-Badger) individuals retained by the Foundry to taste each batch of Float Gas before it ships. Paid in cured salmon. Their job is to detect "the song" — an undefined sensory quality of approved Float Gas.</dd>

          <dt>Foundation Day</dt>
          <dd>Annual league holiday celebrating the inaugural match at Brewer's Reach. The Holiday Festive (League Foundation Hall) biome is in rotation during this event.</dd>

          <dt>The Founding Years</dt>
          <dd>League Years 1 through 8 — the period during which the League's twelve formal teams were progressively admitted (BVR in Year 28, HED in Year 35). Most of the heroes in the Hall of Fallen died during these years, and most of the league's institutional rules (the Crash Rule, the Marshmallow Protocol, the Stadium Wars settlement, the Riot Shield's seven-carrier saga) were established in this period.</dd>

          <dt>Hallowtide</dt>
          <dd>League-wide week-long autumnal event. The Halloween (Reno Hallowtide Hollow) biome is the host venue. Wichita Wolves famously play their best games during Hallowtide.</dd>

          <dt>Hallowtide Tag</dt>
          <dd>The League's only projectile-banned event. Played at the Reno Hallowtide Hollow during Hallowtide week. One knight is "It"; the others flee. Tagging requires a melee strike and freezes the target for three seconds, during which they take heavy bleed damage. The "It" role does not pass — the tagger keeps it. The match ends when only one knight remains alive; ranking is by death order. The Wolves have won every official Hallowtide Tag (codified Year 34). Kor Wartooth is the two-time defending champion. The Pandas have entered every year and have never finished above tenth.</dd>

          <dt>The Hedgehog Tradition</dt>
          <dd>The informal Helena combat circuit that predates HED's formal League admission by several generations. Backyard ranges, neighborhood three-on-three brawls, and mountain-pass exhibition matches gave Hedgehog snipers in particular a sustained training environment outside League oversight. This is why Hester Quillstrike, a rookie in HED's inaugural season (Year 35), was already capable of setting the league's longest-shot record (the 412-Pixel Mark) in her debut year.</dd>

          <dt>The Long Marketing Group (LMG)</dt>
          <dd>Post-Collapse advertising consortium that owns the League's broadcast rights. Slogan: "If it's not on LMG, it didn't happen." Famously antagonistic with the Commissioner's office. Funds half of the Float Foundation in exchange for tax write-offs.</dd>

          <dt>The Marshmallow Protocol</dt>
          <dd>League-wide grenade safety regulation enacted after the Marshmallow Incident in Year 34 of Year 34. Mandates pre-season grenade-safety drills for all teams. Officially named for Felix Marshmallow; informally called "Felix Drills."</dd>

          <dt>The Murder of Pittsburgh</dt>
          <dd>The collective name for the Raven settlement built into the foundry ruins of post-Long-Quiet Pittsburgh. ("Murder" is the corvid collective noun; the Ravens use it without irony.) The Murder is governed by an elder-council known only as the Roost; major decisions require consensus among nine elders. The Pittsburgh Plundering Ravens are the Murder's official League representation. The Murder, as a body, does not bury its dead — cremation in the foundry-fires has been their practice for as long as anyone has counted, including back into the time the Old Ones still walked.</dd>

          <dt>The Antlerwood Rule</dt>
          <dd>League rule, ratified Year 36 founding bell. Designates non-removable bony growths — specifically antlers, horns, and tusks — as <em>attached weapons</em> for the purposes of melee resolution. Named for Bertaud Antlerwood, whose six-foot-four-inch antler span at the Year 36 Caucus's pre-season measurement triggered the original ruling. The rule applies League-wide but, in practice, governs primarily the Moose and the Bison (the latter through a separate clause for horns). The Sharks, who proposed an analogous rule for teeth, were politely deferred on the grounds that teeth are removable.</dd>

          <dt>The Playbook Rotation</dt>
          <dd>Pre-season Caucus tradition codified in the Year 30 Playbook Rotation Rule. Each off-season, every head coach draws a numbered tile from the Caucus's season ballot bag and adopts the corresponding doctrine — one of twenty-five named playbooks ranging from BALANCED through BERSERKER, DOCTRINE, PHALANX, ANARCHIST, GLASS CANNON, etc. — for the upcoming year. Coaches must run their drawn doctrine "in good faith." The system has been challenged three times in formal protest (twice unsuccessfully, once successfully — the Frogs' Year 32 GLASSCANNON re-draw). The Caucus considers the surprise factor essential. Featherquill publishes the full season grid every founding bell.</dd>

          <dt>The Desert Pattern</dt>
          <dd>The Sonora Sly Coyotes' signature engagement tactic, in which one Coyote appears to retreat — repeatedly — drawing opposing knights into believing the Coyote position is collapsing, until six Coyotes engage simultaneously from positions the opposing team had thought were already cleared. The pattern requires precise timing across the entire pack, and has been drilled (per the Sonora pack's training records) eleven thousand times. Coined by Featherquill in her Year 36 founding-bell preview feature; the Coyotes themselves describe the tactic as <em>"asking the desert."</em></dd>

          <dt>The Lynx Solitude</dt>
          <dd>The Yukon Hunting Lynx training tradition, in which each active knight trains alone with a single position-coach for the bulk of the season; the team only forms up on match day. The five active Lynx knights have five separate position-coaches; the team's senior coach (Tessik Snowstep, as of Year 36) reviews training but does not direct it. The League considers the practice unusual but compliant — the rule book requires teams to <em>have</em> training programs, not to specify what they look like.</dd>

          <dt>The Quetzal Nest</dt>
          <dd>The rafter-nest maintained personally by Cintzli of the Yucatan canopy in the Yucatan Jungle-Canopy venue's overgrown rafters. The nest is not formally registered as terrain but functions, in matches at the Yucatan venue, as Cintzli's preferred shooting position. The Caucus has discussed registering the nest on three separate occasions and has, on each occasion, declined to register it on the grounds that doing so would imply the League had built it (the League did not build it; Cintzli built it; the rafters were there before either). The Quetzals have not asked for the nest to be registered; the Caucus has not asked it to be removed; the matter is, by mutual silent agreement, not a matter.</dd>

          <dt>The Northwalk</dt>
          <dd>The journey the Anchorage Polar Bears completed on foot in the Year 35 mid-season — from Anchorage to Brewer's Reach in thirty-two days — to deliver their inclusion application to the League in person. The Polar Bears do not consider the Northwalk a feat. They consider it the courtesy that an application of that gravity required. The League considers it remarkable. Whitepaw, on arrival, is reported to have asked only for water and a chair before reading the application aloud to Whiskerstone. Whiskerstone read the application in silence afterward. The audio of Whitepaw's reading, captured by Treadwell at Whiskerstone's request, is in LMG archive vault 2. It has been requested for public broadcast eleven times. It has been released zero times.</dd>

          <dt>The Pawington Tradition</dt>
          <dd>A Kits-only scavenging ritual where the scavenger kneels by the fallen and asks permission before taking gear. Originated with Mira Pawington. Bench officials have on at least one occasion claimed to hear the corpse <em>respond</em>; that bench official was sent home.</dd>

          <dt>The Pawington Arc</dt>
          <dd>An unusually wide arcing run from flag-pickup back to home base, used by Reka Pawington (Mira's first cousin once removed) during Pawington Cup matches. The arc adds approximately 30% to the direct route distance but consistently evades defenders, who anticipate a straight-line return. Three other Speedsters across the League have attempted to copy the Arc. None have replicated Reka's cap rate. Reka has, on multiple occasions, attributed the Arc to advice received from her late cousin: "the corners watch you. The middle doesn't care." League historians do not know what this means.</dd>

          <dt>The Pawington Cup</dt>
          <dd>The League's flag-running team event, codified Year 33 by Commissioner Whiskerstone after a Mira-vs-Otters incident in which Mira accidentally invented the format. A flag spawns at center; teams compete to carry it back to their own base. The carrier cannot fire and moves at four-fifths speed. First team to five captures wins. Hosted on alternating years by KIT (Hardwood Hall) and BVR (Brewer's Reach Pitch). KIT has won five Cups. BVR has won two. SHK has entered three and won zero, having refused on principle to slow to four-fifths speed.</dd>

          <dt>Permadeath</dt>
          <dd>The condition triggered when a Knight uses up the last of their three lives in a match. Permadeath is final. The Knight's gear drops on the field for survivors to scavenge; their helmet is placed in the Hall of Fallen Heroes; their family receives Float Foundation benefits.</dd>

          <dt>The Reno Heist</dt>
          <dd>The presumed (officially: alleged, possibly imagined) theft of Bristlebeard's Riot Shield in transit to the vault after Year 33's final. The Shield has since been seen on a Raccoon roster, then stolen back, then re-stolen, then re-stolen. Its current location is unknown and is being looked for. The lookers are tired.</dd>

          <dt>Reserve Gas</dt>
          <dd>The lighter, alternative Float Gas formula the Boise Foundry distributed during the Year 33 forty-one-day shutdown. Reserve gas burns cleaner but lifts less; matches played on it have a slightly different feel that veterans claim to detect. The Badgers, who normally receive the heaviest formula and rely on it, finished the Year 33 season 2-12. Reserve Gas is not currently in production. Its formula is not, officially, known to anyone outside the Foundry's senior chemist; unofficially it is widely suspected of being known to whoever wrote the unsigned Foundry letter that arrived in Year 33.</dd>

          <dt>Scavenging</dt>
          <dd>Picking up gear from a fallen Knight on the field. Scavenged gear retains its previous owner's name in the lineage chain (e.g., "Vela's Plate Cuirass"). Items with high scavenge counts become legendary; the most-scavenged item in League history is Bristlebeard's Riot Shield (7 carriers across 6 seasons).</dd>

          <dt>The Stadium Wars</dt>
          <dd>The Year 34 inter-city dispute when Reno, Tampa, and Fresno tried to buy each other's home stadiums. Resolved by Commissioner Whiskerstone, who sat on every contested deed for one consecutive month. Established the permanent League rule that stadiums cannot be sold; this is why neutral venues exist.</dd>

          <dt>The Steward's Pocket</dt>
          <dd>Locker-room shorthand for the bizarre incident in the Year 33 vault rotation, when a steward repeatedly arrived at the vault with a sealed bag containing one fewer item than the bag had been sealed with. The phrase "steward's pocket" now describes any object that goes missing without rational explanation.</dd>

          <dt>Tactical Erasure</dt>
          <dd>Sniper jargon, originating with the Tampa Sharks scouts' shared journal: a kill on a Healer that determines the outcome of an engagement before the engagement has even begun. Many Snipers find the term distasteful but most consider it accurate.</dd>

          <dt>Tactical Self-Sacrifice</dt>
          <dd>The League's official designation for the act of intentionally absorbing fatal damage to deny the kill or its effect to the opposing team. First codified after Old Bristlebeard the First ate a grenade in the inaugural championship final to deny it to the Wolves. Counts as a normal kill in the stats but is decorated separately in the Hall.</dd>

          <dt>The Coalbroke Stop</dt>
          <dd>A bathroom break in transit between the Year 33 final and the League's neutral vault, during which Bristlebeard's Riot Shield is generally agreed to have disappeared from a sealed bag in a parked truck. The truck driver bought a soda. The gas station camera does not point at the truck. Three reporters and one detective have asked. None of them have answers. Locker-room shorthand for "the moment the thing was actually stolen, even though officially nothing was."</dd>

          <dt>Focus Fire</dt>
          <dd>A team tactic, descended from competitive shooter and MOBA play, in which all team members coordinate to attack a single enemy target at the same time. The League's broadcast booth introduced the term in Year 34 after the Owls demonstrated it in a semifinal against the Beavers — five Owl knights independently selected the same wounded Beavers Tank and converged on him within a single round. The Tank had 38 HP. The kill resolved in 1.4 seconds. The Beavers' coach called it "uncomfortably professional." The League's response was to let it happen.</dd>

          <dt>Hold Range</dt>
          <dd>A Sniper's preferred firing distance, generally seventy to ninety percent of their weapon's maximum range. Closer than seventy and they're vulnerable to brawlers; further than ninety and damage falloff makes the shot unreliable. Snipers in Hold Range are said to be "in pocket." Snipers below it are said to be "out of pocket," which is the same expression the Beavers locker room uses to describe knights who are about to embarrass themselves.</dd>

          <dt>Personal Sandbag</dt>
          <dd>A storefront item, introduced Year 35, costing one hundred and fifty bits, applying a fractional speed reduction to one named opposing knight for the duration of a single match. Subject to a long-running ethics debate; the League's official position is that the item is legal sabotage, the Knights' Union's position is that it is sabotage that knights cannot defend against because they cannot detect it, and The Wing Standard's position is that both of these are correct simultaneously.</dd>

          <dt>The Phoenix Heat Clause</dt>
          <dd>A scheduling rule, negotiated Year 30 and revised Year 34, requiring Phoenix-hosted matches between June and mid-September to either start after 7:30pm local OR run under the misting system installed at Skyline Pitch. The clause is responsible for the orange-pink sky that appears in most Foxes home broadcasts, and for the faint soda smell at the field's edge.</dd>

          <dt>Rally Point</dt>
          <dd>The position toward which a wounded knight retreats when their team has a healer or a healthy Tank in the field. Distinct from "running away" — a rally point implies a destination, and a destination implies a plan. The League's broadcast team uses the term to distinguish controlled retreats from panicked ones. Coaches use the term to distinguish a knight who is doing their job from a knight who is not.</dd>

          <dt>Sandbagged Knight</dt>
          <dd>A knight who is performing measurably below their stat sheet for reasons unrelated to injury, fatigue, or known field conditions. The most common cause, since Year 35, is the Personal Sandbag item. The term predates the item — it was originally used to describe knights whose teams had quietly arranged for them to lose, in order to extend the franchise's playoff window. The Commissioner's Office prefers the post-LY-8 usage and has discouraged the older sense.</dd>

          <dt>Pawington Arc</dt>
          <dd>An unusually wide flag-running route, named for Reka Pawington (KIT, rookie Year 35) who used it to set the Pawington Cup's single-match capture record at three captures. The arc takes the carrier near the field's edges instead of straight back to base, adding roughly 30% to the route distance. Defenders consistently fail to anticipate it. Three other Speedsters have attempted the arc; none have replicated the cap rate. Reka has declined to explain why the arc works for her and not for the imitators. Her stated reason is a quote from her aunt Mira: <em>"Mira always said the corners watch you. The middle doesn't care."</em> League historians do not know what this means.</dd>

          <dt>Project Neon Inheritance</dt>
          <dd>The Reno Cultural Office's internal working paper documenting how Reno's lower-Strip survived the Long Quiet. The paper's central finding: a single dedicated power line on the lower Strip stayed lit when the rest of the city went dark, because that line had been installed by the Old Ones' casino consortium specifically to keep slot machines spinning during outages — and the line had been chained to a sub-grid the rest of the city did not know about. Three blocks. Twelve buildings. The Raccoons moved in within "a season" of the Old Ones' disappearance, by the founding-generation oral account; food trade organized along the lit blocks shortly after; engineering guilds gathered in the slot-machine bays within a generation. The original Old-Ones hardware has been replaced and re-replaced across twelve generations of Raccoon engineers; what is unbroken is the continuity of light. The Cultural Office classified the paper internal-only. A junior intern photocopied it in Year 35 and leaked it to The Wing Standard. The Cultural Office has never commented. The intern is now a junior columnist at the same paper. The leak did not damage anyone, the League Library quietly accessioned a copy, and the Cultural Office continues to write polished sentences for orientation pamphlets.</dd>

          <dt>Spawn-Camping</dt>
          <dd>(historical, deprecated since Year 35.) The practice of firing on the opposing spawn line from one's own spawn line at the moment of round commencement. Possible because the original Year 28 field dimensions assumed ranged weapons of the era had effective ranges shorter than the spawn-to-spawn distance. The development of the Railgun in Year 32 invalidated the assumption. Spawn-camping was, for several seasons thereafter, a legal but widely-criticized opening tactic. The Year 35 field-widening — which placed the spawn lines one thousand eighty units apart, two hundred and twenty units beyond the maximum effective range of any current ranged weapon — eliminated the tactic. Coaches now refer to it in past tense, with mild relief.</dd>

          <dt>The Field-Widening</dt>
          <dd>The Year 35 mid-season expansion of the standard match field from 960×540 units to 1280×720 units. The change was announced by Rules Committee bulletin in plain, mildly embarrassed language. Its purpose was to eliminate spawn-camping (see above) and restore a tactical opening phase to each round. The Wolves were unhappy. The Otters were euphoric. Talia Featherquill wrote a column for The Wing Standard. The LMG broadcast team adapted their camera framing within one match. Knights adapted their opening positioning within one season. The field-widening is, by general consensus, the single most consequential rules change in League history that did not require a death to motivate it.</dd>

          <dt>The Crown's Engravings</dt>
          <dd>The Coronation Cup crown was forged by Pell Whittlestone (BDG, retired Year 31) at the close of Year 31 and engraved at her workshop in Boise vernacular script. The League's calligraphers can identify the script as Boise but cannot fully translate it beyond the obvious team-emblem motifs. Whittlestone has declined three formal League requests to translate the engravings, on the grounds that the engravings "are not for the League." A new sigil is added to the rim each season, between Cups. The crown is mailed to Whittlestone after the season closes; she returns it before the next Cup. The League pays in lobster. The accounting is sealed. The current crown carries six sigils — one for each Cup champion — and an additional set of small marks along the inner band that have never appeared in any photograph.</dd>

          <dt>Lobster Standard</dt>
          <dd>The Float Foundation's persistent practice of paying its larger settlements in lobster instead of bits. Treated as eccentric by outside observers and as accounting fact by the Foundation's bookkeepers. The Foundation has one supplier — the Brewer's Reach lobster vendor — and has, on three documented occasions, attempted to acquire a backup supplier; on three occasions the backup supplier has closed shop the next morning, with no explanation, and the lobsters in the secondary fridge have spoiled overnight. The Foundation has stopped trying. Pell Whittlestone (the crown forger) bills exclusively in lobster. So does at least one independent contractor at the Boise Foundry. So does, by implication and the records of three settled lawsuits, the Wing Standard's own publication office. The Lobster Standard is, by every reasonable measure, the League's secondary currency. The Commissioner has not formally acknowledged this. The Commissioner's ledgers have.</dd>

          <dt>Bristlebeard Pattern</dt>
          <dd>The well-documented Beaver Tank tradition in which the team's anchoring Tank takes the surname Bristlebeard, charges directly at the first enemy line they see, and dies in their first or second season. The First died in Year 28 R5, taking three opposing Beavers with him. The Second died on the opening kickoff of Year 32. The Third — Bjorn Bristlebeard, currently active — has, as of this writing, broken the pattern by playing a defensive back line and surviving eight matches into Year 35. The Beaver fanbase is split between those who want the pattern restored and those who want Bjorn to live. Bjorn is twenty-two. Bjorn carries the First's Riot Shield. The Foundation has offered to vault the Shield. Bjorn has declined. The fanbase notices.</dd>

          <dt>The Wave Doctrine</dt>
          <dd>The Caucus's Year-36 ratified rule that, in continuous-mode tournaments (Crown, Capture-the-Pole, Tag), downed knights of a given team return to the field <em>together, as a wave</em>, on a fixed delay, rather than as individuals on rolling timers. The doctrine includes a slowest-knight sprint allowance: the slowest knight in the wave is granted a temporary speed adjustment so the wave does not stretch out into a disorganized trickle on the way to the center engagement. The doctrine's stated purpose is to prevent the snowball — the runaway score lead a team accumulated under the previous individual-return system once they had a numerical advantage at the crown. By the second sanctioned application of the doctrine (RCC vs PLR, Year 36 R2 Crown), the doctrine had produced two consecutive comeback wins for the trailing team. The Caucus's tactical analyst Pell Whittlestone has called the rule <em>"the second-largest single-rule contribution to the League's tactical balance since the Marshmallow Protocol"</em> and is, by her own admission, "still not certain whether that ranking is too high or too low."</dd>

          <dt>L'Ancrage</dt>
          <dd>The Saint-Laurent Antlerlords' tank-class tradition: the team's anchoring Tank — currently Théodred Brisefer III — stands in the center of the pitch as a stationary tactical anchor while the other four Antlerlord knights rotate around him in concentric arcs. The position name translates from the Saint-Laurent native creole as "The Anchor." The role is, technically, just a Moose; the Antlerlords' tank assignment under League rules has no separate plate kit because the Moose's own mass and antler rack constitute the kit. The current L'Ancrage is approximately one and three-quarters of an Old-Ones cargo lorry by the Caucus's mass register; the Caucus has not been able to measure him precisely because their measurement scale ends at one cargo lorry. He has, by Antlerlords' coaching account, never lost a one-on-one engagement on a sanctioned field. Opposing teams have, by tactical necessity, started organizing their pitch geometry around his standing point — even when they intend not to engage him directly.</dd>

          <dt>The Drift / la borradura / el sexto</dt>
          <dd>The Sonora Coyotes' signature tactical pattern. A Coyote Speedster, mid-engagement, appears to retreat — unhurriedly, in a wide arc, in a manner that the opposing team's tactical attention reads as <em>"that knight has left the engagement"</em>. The Coyote then drifts behind cover at the perimeter and, by the opposing team's perception, ceases to exist on the tactical map. Coach Reyes of CYT calls this <em>la borradura</em> ("the erasure"). With four Coyotes drifting simultaneously across an engagement, the opposing team's perception of the field collapses to one or two visible Coyotes — and, when the drift reverses and the Coyotes re-engage from their drift positions, the opposing team's tactical map registers a sixth Coyote that was not, in fact, ever there. Reyes calls this <em>el sexto</em> ("the sixth"). The Coyotes have, by Caucus statistical record, never fielded more than five active knights in a sanctioned match. The opposing team always counts six.</dd>

          <dt>The Cold Stones</dt>
          <dd>A small, very heavy stone trophy commissioned by the Caucus and forged by Pell Whittlestone of Boise for the annual Frostfall Friendly between the Polar Bears (PLR) and the Lynx (LYX). The trophy was named at the suggestion of both teams' captains, who — when asked separately and not consulting each other — proposed the same name on the grounds that <em>"there are stones, and they are cold; there is, frankly, no need to elaborate."</em> The Caucus took this as a quorum and adopted the name. The trophy is held by the winning team for the duration of the year and is required, under the Friendly's rules, to be stored in a venue's coldest available chamber for the entire holding period. The first Cold Stones is, as of Year 36, in the Anchorage settlement's ice-archive. The Lynx have requested visitation rights. The Polar Bears have, in good humor, declined.</dd>

          <dt>The Frosthold Pitch</dt>
          <dd>The Boise venue selected by the Caucus as the official neutral-ground for the Cold Stones Frostfall Friendly. Distinguished by its central feature: a long ridge of low ice that runs north-south down the middle of the pitch, which deteriorates over the course of a match into a series of low pillars, then into a flat surface, depending on how heavily the round has trampled it. The ridge is not, by League rule, considered a permanent terrain feature; it is, in practice, the most influential single piece of cover on any League pitch, on the grounds that it is constantly changing under play. The Caucus has discussed regulating the ridge. The Caucus has, on each occasion, decided not to regulate the ridge, on the grounds that <em>"the ridge is the venue; we cannot regulate the venue without rebuilding the venue; we are not in the rebuilding-venues business this season."</em></dd>

          <dt>The Snowball / The Snowball Break</dt>
          <dd>A pre-Wave-Doctrine pattern in continuous-mode (Crown / Capture-the-Pole / Tag) matches. Once a team gathered a numerical lead at the active scoring objective, the lead snowballed: opposing knights returning to the field one at a time on rolling timers walked into a numerically superior defensive line and were knocked back out before they could mount a coordinated re-engagement. The trailing team's individual-return knights walked into a wall. The wall held. The wall scored. The match was, by minute three, decided. The <em>Snowball Break</em> is the inverse — the moment, under the Wave Doctrine, when the trailing team's wave returns in formation and breaks the leading team's wall. The two have become a paired tactical concept across the League's coaching literature: the snowball is the failure mode the doctrine fixes, the break is the success mode the doctrine produces. Coach Reyes of CYT, asked which he prefers as a coaching concept, answered: <em>"I prefer the break. I am, however, a Coyote. We have always been the trailing team in these matches. We have always wanted the wall to break. The Polar Bears, who have been the wall, prefer the snowball, and that is fair, and we will fight them about it next bracket."</em></dd>

          <dt>The Loambright Correction</dt>
          <dd>A standard taught at the Caucus's annual sniper-class workshop: <em>do not, when shooting at a non-Healer target, choose a firing line that intersects the path of an opposing Healer at any point in the projectile's travel.</em> Named for Avery Loambright, the Hedgehog Healer who was killed in the Year 33 Brewer's Reach Final by a Beaver Sniper round meant for the Wolves' Striker Crash Wartooth. The shooter, Bristlebeard the Second, has not — in eight subsequent seasons — taken another shot whose line intersected an opposing Healer's path. The correction is, by every Caucus archery instructor's account, the single most-respected unwritten standard in the sport. The League has not, formally, written it down. The League's snipers do not, by an informal agreement that has survived three different head archery instructors, need it written down.</dd>

          <dt>The Bow</dt>
          <dd>The Wolf-pack post-kill ritual, originated at the Year 33 Brewer's Reach Final. After a fallen opponent goes down — either in match or in subsequent visits to the Hall of Fallen Heroes — the Wolves on the field briefly form a circle around the body or the chalk mark and the captain bows. The bow lasts eleven seconds. The duration was set on its first observation and has not, by Wolves' captain Halfmoon Greylane's stated commitment, ever varied. Not adopted by any other team. The Wolves themselves consider it a form of acknowledgment, not apology. The canonical explanation, from a fan letter <em>"On the Bow"</em> reprinted in <em>The Long Bow</em>, vol. 2, is that the bow is wolf physics — the fallen opponent is, briefly, part of the pack's pattern, and the pattern requires acknowledgment. Greylane has never publicly explained the bow. She has, when asked, said only: <em>"The bow is a Wolf thing. It is not for me to explain. It is for the body to receive."</em></dd>

          <dt>Greylane's Carry</dt>
          <dd>The Year 35 quarterfinal in which Wolves' captain Halfmoon Greylane carried a downed Healer (Pinedrift) across forty-eight paces of open pitch under sustained fire from two opposing Snipers and a Brawler. Greylane took fourteen separate hit registers, three of which dropped her HP into the red, and did not return fire during the carry. Pinedrift survived. The match playback is in the Caucus's tactical archive under the file name <em>"Greylane carry — do not edit"</em> — the most-viewed playback in the archive, by Foundation steward measurement. Greylane has refused to allow the Wolves' coaching staff to use it as a training video. Her own statement on the record: <em>"That was not a teaching moment. That was the only thing I knew how to do. The Healer's name is Pinedrift. The Healer is alive. That is the lesson, if you need a lesson. I would prefer you did not need a lesson."</em></dd>

          <dt>The Wide Draw</dt>
          <dd>A Cleveland Boulder Badgers tactical pattern, drilled into the team's Year 36 training camp by head coach Brockholm Slatebrush. Functionally identical to the Coyotes' drift pattern (la borradura), but renamed by Slatebrush so the Badgers — who would not, by their own coaching staff's frank admission, willingly run a tactic called "the drift" — would adopt it. The Caucus's tactical archive has not, formally, recognized the equivalence. Slatebrush has not, formally, denied the equivalence. Featherquill, asked off the record, said: <em>"The Badgers are running the Coyote tactic and calling it something else. The Coyotes have noticed. The Coyotes are flattered. The Coyotes are also planning to drift around the wide draw, which is a thing only the Coyotes know how to do, and which will be, in the Badgers' R7 match against the Antlerlords, an interesting moment for both teams."</em></dd>

          <dt>The Long Marketing Group / LMG</dt>
          <dd>The League's exclusive broadcast partner, holding rights to all sanctioned-match coverage. Slogan: <em>"If it's not on LMG, it didn't happen."</em> Operates the broadcast booth and the kinetics tracker (the official kill-line measurement system used to verify long-shot records). Funds approximately forty percent of the Float Foundation's operating budget. Holds the only authorized set of cameras at every venue. Does not, by formal League rule, control which matches are broadcast — but does, by its own stated editorial discretion, decline to broadcast some matches per season for "format coherence" reasons that the LMG is reluctant to elaborate on. The Beaver coaching staff has, in private, accused the LMG of selective non-broadcast (see the unprinted musing <em>"On the Long Marketing Group"</em>). The LMG has not, formally, responded to the accusation. The Sharks have lost three matches that were, on paper, training matches. The Beavers have won two of those. The standings reflect what the LMG broadcast.</dd>

          <dt>The Vendor</dt>
          <dd>The lobster vendor on Concession Row at Brewer's Reach Pitch. Has been at her booth since before the inaugural match (Year 28) and has not, for any reason, ever moved her booth. Her prices have not changed since the League's founding — one bit per lobster, with the small wax cup of melted butter included. The Float Foundation's sole lobster supplier, by long-standing tradition. Refuses, on every Foundation request, to raise her prices to match the Foundation's official concession-stand pricing. The Foundation has, on three occasions, requested that she do so. She has, on three occasions, declined. The Foundation has, on three occasions, declined to close the booth. Her name is not, by long-standing personal preference, on any Foundation document. The Foundation refers to her, in formal correspondence, as <em>"the Vendor."</em> The Vendor is, by the Brewer's Reach Reader column <em>"On the Vendor Who Has Not Moved,"</em> the longest-serving institution in the entire Float Knights organization — older than the Commissioner, older than the LMG broadcast booth, older than Pell Whittlestone's Foundry, older than the founding match itself.</dd>

          <dt>The Hall of Fallen Heroes</dt>
          <dd>A long, narrow room in the Foundation Hall (Boston) maintained by the Float Foundation. Lists, in order of permadeath, every Knight who has ever been recorded as permadeceased on a sanctioned League field. Eight rows of names, at this writing, with room for forty more rows. Visited by every Wolves' active line at the start of every season's Brewer's Reach match — the captain bows for eleven seconds at Avery Loambright's name (third row from the door, sixth name) and the line follows. The Bears, the Antlerlords, the Lynx, and the Quetzals have, since their respective League entries, observed similar visits with their own teams' fallen — the Bears' visit takes the form of a single shared minute of held breath; the Antlerlords' visit takes the form of a slow, deep nod from L'Ancrage that lasts (by Foundation steward measurement) twenty-three seconds; the Lynx visit individually, in rotation across the whole pre-season, never as a group; the Quetzals have not, as of Year 36, lost a knight to permadeath, and so do not yet have a Hall ritual. The Foundation has set aside, against the Quetzals' wishes, a row for them anyway. The Quetzals have not protested.</dd>

          <dt>The Raccoon Dignity</dt>
          <dd>The Raccoons' annual post-Coronation-Cup ritual, established by Dustpaw Trashbright at the inaugural Cup in Year 31 and continued by every subsequent Raccoon captain. On winning the Cup, the captain accepts the brass crown on the broadcast post-match line, makes a brief statement that includes the phrase <em>"I will be taking it home,"</em> and transports the crown — by team transport, at speed — toward Pittsburgh. The crown is then, on every winning year, recovered the following morning at Moss Quickfingers' Reno pawn shop, where it has been stored overnight in exchange for a small lobster fee. The Foundation has built a recurring annual budget line for the recovery. The line is called <em>"crown retrieval logistics"</em> and amounts, annually, to four lobsters and a small storage fee. The practice has, in six of eight Cup years, occurred on schedule. (The two non-Raccoon Cup wins did not, by the winning teams' respective decisions, involve any pawning.) The Foundation has stopped commenting on the practice. Featherquill has called it <em>"the cleanest sport I have ever covered."</em></dd>

          <dt>Quickfingers' Reno Storage</dt>
          <dd>The Reno pawn shop owned by Moss Quickfingers (a beaver of unknown allegiance, sixteen-year shop-tenure), at which the Coronation Cup brass crown has, by the Raccoons' annual practice, been deposited overnight every Cup year the Raccoons have won. The shop's official function is general pawnbroking; the crown is the only item Quickfingers is on record as accepting from the same client every year, and the only item he has ever stored under the same pawn ticket-name (a member of the active Raccoon roster, varying by year). The shop accepts payment for storage in lobster only. Quickfingers has, in three separate interviews, declined to comment on whether the practice is technically pawning, layaway, or some informal hybrid. He has said only: <em>"The crown is at my shop. The Foundation knows where it is. The Raccoons know where it is. I am paid in lobster. The lobster is good. I have stopped asking questions."</em> The shop is on Reno's South Strip, between a tobacconist and a tea-and-coffee importer; it has not, in sixteen years, been moved.</dd>

          <dt>The LMG Translator</dt>
          <dd>The single staff position at the LMG broadcast booth dedicated to multilingual translation of pre-match, post-match, and sideline interviews from non-League-Common-speaking teams. Currently held by Estelle Roiseau-Manchot (Saint-Laurent goose), who handles Saint-Laurent creole (Antlerlords), the Lynx language (when Lynx captains consent to be interviewed at all), and the Yucatan Spanish creole half of Quetzals' interviews. Trees-language Quetzals interviews are not, currently, translated by the position; the LMG has not yet hired a trees-language translator. Roiseau-Manchot's working method is rigorous non-summarization: she renders the source ambiguity in the target language and lets the captain's own words do the talking. She is paid in mixed bits and lobster, with the lobster portion the largest individual lobster-payment line item in the Foundation's books — a fact the Foundation has, on three occasions, attempted to convert to bits for streamlining and which Roiseau-Manchot has, on three occasions, declined.</dd>

          <dt>The Tinkerbarrel Disclosure</dt>
          <dd>The serial publication, in <em>The Lobster Reach Daily</em> across Year 33's spring quarter, of retired Sharks equipment manager Reef Tinkerbarrel's career memoir, including the eighth installment which contained the full text of his Year 30 R3 equipment-manager logbook documenting the Sharks' undeclared use of a flat (under-pressure) Float Gas batch in their home shutout of the Foxes. The disclosure prompted the Year 33 Caucus working session at which the Year 30 R3 result was — over the Foxes' formal objection — allowed to stand, on Whittlestone's argument that the exploit was a Foundry-side delivery failure no team in Year 30 had the technical capability to remediate properly, and that the Foundry's Year-31 protocol upgrade had eliminated the exploit's feasibility. The disclosure also produced the eighth installment's most-read print run in the publication's twenty-three-year history — the print run had to be doubled mid-week. Tinkerbarrel did not, on disclosure, request payment from the publication beyond his standard memoir serialization rate. He has, by his post-retirement statement, no further memoirs in preparation.</dd>

          <dt>The Roving Anchor</dt>
          <dd>An experimental Antlerlords tactical formation in which L'Ancrage (the team's anchoring Tank) abandons his stationary center-pitch stance and joins the perimeter rotation as a slow-moving fifth knight. By every Caucus analyst's pre-existing tactical literature, the formation is theoretically possible but practically compromised — L'Ancrage's mass is a feature of his stationary stance, and a moving L'Ancrage cannot, by his own walking speed, sustain the rotation's pacing. The formation was first deployed in a sanctioned match in Year 36 R7 (BDG vs MOS at the Cleveland Boulder Pitch), in real-time response to the Badgers' Wide Draw tactical debut, with no prior team drill. The Antlerlords lost the match 4-1. The formation has not, by Antlerlords' coaching staff's pre-Year-37 commitment, been retired; it is being drilled into the team's off-season exhibition schedule and is, by Marc-Olivier Brisefer's stated intent, expected to debut in fully-drilled form in Year 37's regular season.</dd>

          <dt>The Crab Standard</dt>
          <dd>The Tampa Bay vendor district's preferred currency unit, alongside but distinct from the lobster. The Crab Standard is, by Foundation accountancy informal practice, treated at a floating rate against the lobster — the Year 33 Tampa ledger records 1.4 fresh-caught crabs per lobster as a typical week's rate, with day-old or ice-stored crab dropping to 0.9. The Crab Standard is the operating currency for the Tampa Bay venue's concession row, the Olympia harbor canteen (which imports Tampa-caught crab weekly), and three Reno restaurants of repute. The Foundation does not officially recognize cross-currency exchange; the Foundation's accountancy office, when asked about the practice, has on three occasions said only that it "does not officially recognize" the exchange. The accountancy office uses the exchange table every Friday. Splashfang &amp; Sisters of Tampa (est. Year 24) supply approximately seventy percent of the in-circulation Crab Standard. The remainder is informal — backyard catches, fishing-cooperative submissions, and a small but steady contribution from a single Olympia harbor docker who goes out alone most Sunday mornings and is, by every honest account, the source of the highest-quality crab in the entire continental supply chain. He has, on multiple occasions, declined to scale his operation. He has said, when asked: <em>"I am one otter with one boat. I will, by my own commitment, remain one otter with one boat. The crab will be what the crab is. I do not want the work."</em></dd>

          <dt>The Clam Ledger</dt>
          <dd>The freshwater secondary currency, used primarily in cities along major river systems — Pittsburgh (Allegheny basin), Saint-Laurent (the entire freshwater outflow), Helena (glacier-runoff streams), and Boise (Snake River tributaries). The Clam Ledger trades at approximately four to six clams per lobster, depending on shucking status, source water, and seasonal availability. The Saint-Laurent freshwater clam — smaller than the Pittsburgh variety, six per lobster — has, since the Antlerlords' Year 36 admission, become the dominant in-League freshwater currency by volume, on the strength of a single decision by the Foundation accountancy to accept the smaller variety at par with the Pittsburgh variety for vendor-staff payroll purposes. The Pittsburgh Ravens' equipment foundry has, since Year 36 R3, accepted Saint-Laurent clams as payment for League-spec arrows; the Antlerlords, in turn, have accepted Pittsburgh-foundry arrows as payment for visiting-team lodging at the Saint-Laurent venue. The arrangement is, by every Foundation accounting officer's read, "the cleanest cross-team freshwater barter the League has ever produced. We are not, formally, recognizing it. We are, in practice, paying half our Saint-Laurent venue payroll in Pittsburgh arrows."</dd>

          <dt>The Crawfish Pile</dt>
          <dd>The Bayou Tigers' export currency, formalized as a unit at the Year 33 first-export volume of six crawfish per pile. The crawfish-pile-of-six trades at approximately 1.2 lobsters by Year 33 ledger; the rate has held within ten percent across the three years of formal export. The Crawfish Pile is the operating currency for the Bayou Cypress-Hollow venue's concessions, all of New Orleans' delta-basin food markets, and (informally) the Tampa Bay vendor district's late-season trade when the local crab catch is short. The Tigers' export operation is run by a single bayou cooperative — the Stripeshoulder family's extended household, which maintains the catch traps along the bayou's outer rim — and the cooperative has, in three years, never missed a weekly export shipment to Tampa. Stripeshoulder herself has, in interviews, declined to discuss the export operation in any detail; her stated reason is that <em>"the crawfish are the bayou's. The bayou gives them. We pass them along. The discussion of how, frankly, would not be a discussion. It would be the bayou's, not ours. We are not, in this matter, qualified to speak."</em></dd>

          <dt>The Oyster Tab</dt>
          <dd>The Yucatan-sourced tropical-ocean currency, used primarily at the Yucatan Jungle-Canopy venue's concessions and (since Year 36) at the Concession Row in-shell oyster cart that the lobster vendor herself sponsored, on the grounds that <em>"the lobster is one bit; the oyster is something else; the something else needs its own booth, and I am not adding the something else to my booth, but the something else is good and people should be able to buy it. I am introducing the Quetzals' supplier to the Foundation. The Foundation will handle it from here. I do not, on this matter, need to be involved further."</em> Oysters trade at approximately 0.7 lobsters per oyster, in-shell, requiring shucker — the rate is high on a per-unit basis because the Yucatan-sourced oyster is, by every culinary read, exceptional, and the shucking is, by professional oyster-shucker rate, additional. The Oyster Tab is the only currency in Foundation accountancy's books that has a formal supplemental fee for skilled labor (the shucking fee, paid in lobster, two units per dozen oysters). The fee was negotiated by the Quetzals' coaching staff on behalf of the supplier, who is a single Yucatan jungle-floor opossum named Rosalva Jirónsalado. Jirónsalado does not, by her own preference, ever travel to non-Yucatan venues. The shucking, when oysters are shipped to Concession Row, is done by a contracted shucker the Foundation has retained — by her recommendation — at the standard fee.</dd>

          <dt>The Southern Continent</dt>
          <dd>The continent south of the Yucatan extension, comprising (by the basin coordinating council's Year 35 letter to the Yucatan League outpost) twenty-three settled lizard-line communities, eleven alligator-line communities, fourteen serpentine-line communities, and an indeterminate number of tropical bird communities. The League has, in three rounds of formal correspondence, attempted to extend admission to southern teams. The basin coordinating council has, in three rounds of formal response, politely declined. Stated reasons: travel distance (the Continental Rail does not connect south of the Yucatan extension; funding for a southern connection is not, by either side, available); predator-prey unease (the League's existing rosters include several species lines that register as predators in southern jungle ecology, and the southern serpentine communities have indicated they would prefer not to share locker tunnels with Lynx); and climate adaptation (the Helena Glacier Rink would be, by the southern coordinator's own assessment, lethal to a basin lizard within forty minutes of arrival). The coordinating council has, in its third response, extended a standing invitation: the League is welcome to play exhibition matches at southern venues — Lima Highlands Pitch, Caracas Canopy Hall, Buenos Aires Wetlands — and the southern communities will host hospitably. The League has not, as of Year 36, exercised the invitation. The Foundation has retained the option for a future season's pre-season exhibition slate.</dd>

          <dt>Lima Highlands Pitch</dt>
          <dd>A southern continent venue, located in the high mountain plateau of what the Old Ones called Lima. Maintained by the Lima lizard-line community (basin variety, descended from a continuous population that survived the Long Quiet at altitude). The pitch is, by the southern coordinator's brief description in the standing invitation, <em>"a flat stone court at altitude, with mountain wind, and a sun the northern teams will need to acclimate to."</em> The League's pre-Year-37 exhibition schedule has the venue listed as a possible exhibition slot. No date has been set. The community has, in correspondence, indicated that they would be honored to host. The community has, in the same correspondence, indicated that they will not, in any case, send a team north.</dd>

          <dt>Caracas Canopy Hall</dt>
          <dd>A southern continent venue, located in the upper canopy of the tropical jungle north of what the Old Ones called Caracas. Maintained by the Caracas tropical-bird community (multiple species, organized by canopy level rather than by team). The Hall is, by the southern coordinator's description, <em>"more rafters than venue. The northern teams' Snipers would, by canopy structure, find the venue accommodating. The northern teams' Tanks would, by canopy structure, find the venue impossible. We are, in extending the invitation, suggesting that the League consider a Sniper-roster-only exhibition match at the Hall. We will, in such a match, host with our own Snipers; the matchup would be, by every honest reading, lopsided in our favor; we are willing to accept this asymmetry as the cost of hospitality. The League is welcome to decline."</em> The League has, as of Year 36, neither accepted nor declined.</dd>

          <dt>Buenos Aires Wetlands</dt>
          <dd>A southern continent venue, located in the river-delta wetlands south of what the Old Ones called Buenos Aires. Maintained by the wetlands alligator-line community. The venue is, by the southern coordinator's description, <em>"a venue where every match would be played in approximately ankle-deep water, regardless of season. The water is the venue. The northern teams will, on visiting, need to plan accordingly. We are honored, in any case, to host."</em> The Sharks' coaching staff has, on receipt of the invitation, expressed informal interest. The Sharks have not formally requested the exhibition match; the Caucus has not, in any case, scheduled one. The Sharks are, by Caucus analyst's read, the most likely League team to eventually visit, on the grounds that they are the only team currently rostered whose archetype-line is comfortable in standing water. The alligators are, by every available account, comfortable hosting them; the Sharks are, by every available account, comfortable visiting; the trip is, by either's account, expensive.</dd>

          <dt>The Vendor's Bell</dt>
          <dd>A small brass bell at the corner of the lobster vendor's booth at Brewer's Reach Pitch's Concession Row. The bell is rung by the vendor, by long-standing personal practice, when a child purchases their first lobster from her stall. The bell rings once. The vendor does not announce the ring. The vendor does not, by any accessible record, count the rings. The bell has been at the booth since the booth opened. The bell's clapper, by Foundation steward measurement, has worn approximately four millimeters of brass over eight seasons. The bell will, by reasonable extrapolation, last approximately three more lifetimes at this rate. The vendor has not, by any account, ever moved the bell from its corner. The bell rings, by booth steward's count, on average twice per match-day. The total ring count is, by no one's count, a knowable number. The bell rings. The child gets a piece of paper, in extraordinary circumstances. The child, in ordinary circumstances, gets a lobster, melted butter, and a moment in which a vendor sees them and rings a bell. This is enough.</dd>

          <dt>Pinedrift the Survivor</dt>
          <dd>A Wolves' Healer who, in the Year 35 quarterfinal at Olympia, was downed by Sniper fire and carried by Halfmoon Greylane across forty-eight paces of open pitch under sustained Sniper fire to the bench medical strip. Pinedrift survived. He has, in subsequent seasons, returned to the active roster as a healer. He has, in subsequent seasons, played in seventeen matches. He has not, in any subsequent match, allowed himself to be downed in open pitch — he plays a careful Healer's game, with cover priority, that the Wolves' coaching staff has, in private, called <em>"the Pinedrift adjustment"</em> and which the staff teaches to every new Wolves' Healer as a baseline habit. Pinedrift has, in five known interviews, declined to discuss the carry. He has said only, on the record: <em>"I was carried. I am alive. The captain did the carrying. The captain has, on this matter, said all that needs to be said. I will not, by my own preference, add to it."</em> He has, by his coaching staff's quiet record, sent Greylane a small handwritten card every year on the anniversary of the carry. The card, by Greylane's quiet record, is, in every year, the first piece of mail she opens that day.</dd>

          <dt>Whitefang the Suspected</dt>
          <dd>A name appearing in graffiti throughout Brewer's Reach Pitch and (by sporadic report) at six other venues across the continent. Whitefang is not, by any League record, a knight. Whitefang is not, by any team record, a player. Whitefang's existence is unconfirmed. Whitefang's signature appears, by Foundation cleaner records, in three different handwritings across at least four seasons of bathroom-stall and locker-tunnel scribblings. The Foundation has, on six occasions, attempted to identify the writer (or writers); the Foundation has, on six occasions, given up. Whitefang is, by every honest reading, a running collaborative joke maintained by an unknown number of fans across multiple cities. The Foundation has stopped trying to clean the writings off completely. The Foundation now, by long-standing janitor preference, leaves the most-recent Whitefang scribble intact and only cleans the older ones. The result is that Brewer's Reach has, at any given moment, exactly one Whitefang scribble visible, somewhere in the building. The most recent (Year 36 R5) is in the third stall of the men's washroom in the upper concourse, in red gel-pen, and reads: <em>"WHITEFANG WAS NEVER HERE — and was here anyway"</em>.</dd>

          <dt>The Felix Drills</dt>
          <dd>The unofficial in-locker-room name for the grenade-safety training that became mandatory across the League after the Year 34 Marshmallow Incident. The drills are named for Felix Marshmallow, the Pandas' Tank who was killed by friendly grenade fire in mid-match — the formal protocol bears the team's name, the drills bear his. Pre-season camp, every team, every year: a Grenadier-class knight stands at the center of the practice circle holding a defused training grenade. The line walks past in single file. Each knight, on passing, repeats the same four words aloud — <em>"the grenade is yours."</em> The Grenadier responds, also aloud — <em>"the grenade is mine."</em> The line continues. The drill takes, by stopwatch, roughly four minutes per team per season. The drill has not, in three subsequent seasons, prevented every grenade incident; it has, by Caucus statistical record, reduced friendly-grenade casualties by approximately seventy percent. The Pandas' coaching staff continues to attend the drill in person every season. They do not, in attendance, run the drill themselves; they observe. Felix's family has, every season since Year 34, sent the Pandas' bench a small plate of marshmallows on the morning of the drill. The marshmallows are eaten. The plate is returned. The plate has been returned, by tradition, with a single sentence written on its underside: <em>"the grenade is ours."</em> The plate has, in three years, never come back blank. The family has, in three years, never asked who is writing on it.</dd>

          <dt>The Crash Rule</dt>
          <dd>An equipment standard adopted League-wide after Year 34, requiring all Wolves Brawlers to wear heavy plate. The rule is named for Crash Wartooth, who, in Year 34 R3, was stunned three times in twelve seconds by an Owls' bench-coach-coordinated focus-fire engagement that exposed a gap in the Wolves' Brawler kit. Wartooth survived the round but tore a knee tendon, missed eight matches in recovery, and returned the next season, by his coaching staff's careful management, in heavier plate than the kit he had left in. The rule was proposed by the Wolves' coaching staff at the Year 34 off-season working session and adopted by the Caucus as a Wolves-only standard within four hours of submission — the fastest single rule-change ratification in League history. The rule does not apply to other teams' Brawlers; the Wolves do not, by their own coaching staff's preference, want it to. <em>"It is our rule. The plate is our plate. The pack is the pack. The other teams will, in their own time, decide what their Brawlers need to wear. We will not, on the record, recommend."</em> Wartooth, asked years later about the rule, said only: <em>"It is heavier. I am older. The two adjustments fit together. I do not, on the matter, have a stronger opinion. The rule is the rule. I am still on the line."</em></dd>
        </dl>
